title: World number one Sabalenka ousted in Toronto by Alexandrova
description: TORONTO: World number one Aryna Sabalenka was eliminated by Russian 16th seed Ekaterina Alexandrova on Saturday in a fourth-round match at the WTA Toronto Masters tournament.Alexandrova defeated the four-time Grand Slam winner from...
content: Published August 09, 2026 TORONTO: World number one Aryna Sabalenka was eliminated by Russian 16th seed Ekaterina Alexandrova on Saturday in a fourth-round match at the WTA Toronto Masters tournament. Alexandrova defeated the four-time Grand Slam winner from Belarus 7-6 (7/3), 4-6, 6-4 in 2hr 29min to book a berth in the quarter-finals. Sabalenka, who will seek her third consecutive US Open title next month, fell to 5-5 in her career WTA rivalry with Alexandrova, who will face either American eighth seed Amanda Anisimova or Ukraine's ninth-seeded Elina Svitolina in the quarter-finals. Sabalenka broke for a 2-0 lead in the opening set, dropped the next four games, then held and broke back to 4-4 on a forehand drop volley winner. Double faults by Sabalenka in the 11th game and Alexandrova in the 12th surrendered breaks leading to a tie-break. The Russian took five of the last six points to seal the first set when Sabalenka swatted a crosscourt forehand wide. In the second set, Alexandrova hit a forehand long to surrender a break and give Sabalenka a 4-3 lead. The top seed then held serve twice to force a decider. Sabalenka was broken when she netted a forehand to give Alexandrova a 3-1 edge, but the Russian double-faulted away a break in the seventh game. In the 10th game, Sabalenka made three unforced errors to give Alexandrova break and match points. Sabalenka saved the first on a service winner and the second on an ace. But after sending a backhand beyond the baseline, the Belarusian made her sixth and final double fault to lose the match. "I didn't have any expectations before the match," Alexandrova said. "I knew it was going to be super difficult when I walked on the court. "I was trying to risk as much as possible because it felt like it was the only way to create some chances. It caused many more mistakes but at the same time I created many more opportunities." Copyright © 2026. Geo Television Network. All Rights Reserved. | Contact Us | Authors | Privacy Policy

title: World's oceans hit record-high July temperatures - BBC News
description: Global oceans recorded their hottest July on record, partly fuelled by developing El Niño conditions, as wildfires continue to ravage western Europe.
content: The world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, partly fuelled by developing El Niño conditions in the Pacific , according to the EU's climate monitoring service. The average sea surface temperature (SST) outside the world's polar regions - between 60 degrees north and 60 degrees south - was 20.96C last month, beating the previous high of 20.89C, set in 2023. Last month was the joint second-warmest July globally on record, with temperatures 1.47C above the estimated pre-industrial average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service. Meanwhile, Western Europe experienced its hottest ever June and July, with prolonged hot and dry conditions fuelling extreme wildfires across the region. Elsewhere, the UK is braced for its fifth heatwave of the year this week , as persistent dry weather puts further pressure on water supplies and could see more areas officially declared in drought. What is El Niño and why could it mean record temperatures? Rhine falls to record low levels as drought strains Europe's rivers Around Europe, sea surface temperatures in July reached record highs along the Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean, contributing to widespread strong and severe marine heatwaves. Sea temperatures remained exceptionally high across much of the tropical Pacific, where El Niño conditions are developing and forecast to strengthen in the coming months. El Niño is a natural weather pattern in the Pacific that combined with human-driven global warming can cause temperature spikes and more extreme weather. Oceans are a vital regulator of the climate, absorbing most of the excess heat generated by greenhouse gas emissions and producing half of Earth's oxygen. The greatest effect of ocean warming is on sea level rise. As seawater warms it expands, and this thermal expansion accounts for roughly a third of sea level rise recorded by scientists to date. That water encroaches on low-lying coasts and island nations. Hotter seas are also driving longer and fiercer marine heatwaves, which have bleached coral reefs on a mass scale and decimated kelp forests and fisheries. Warmer ocean surfaces also evaporate more heat and moisture into the air, intensifying tropical storms and loading them with heavier rainfall. Western Europe is experiencing an exceptional run of extreme heat - with record-breaking temperatures in June and July, and some areas facing their third or fourth heat wave since May. The average temperature across western Europe for June and July was 21.62C - 2.79C above average and the highest for the two-month period. "July 2026 was the third consecutive month of exceptional heat in western Europe," said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. Persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over the region, she said, while dry soils reduced the ability to provide natural cooling. "This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another," she added. France, Spain, parts of Germany and the UK recorded exceptionally low rainfall and/or soil moisture, while soil moisture levels across much of western Europe were significantly lower than in 2022, when the region experienced severe drought. River levels have been much lower than average - in some places exceptionally low -with the Seine, Rhine and Danube among those particularly affected. Low flows exacerbate pressure on water supplies and irrigation, aquatic ecosystems, river transport and energy production. Some rivers in Europe have recorded extremely low water levels, including the Danube The prolonged hot and dry conditions have created favourable conditions for wildfires, with massive wildfires raging across western Europe last month and "exceptional activity" in terms of the area burned and smoke and emissions generated. "Climate change is increasingly bringing the kinds of hot and dry conditions that favour large, high-intensity wildfires in southern Europe while extended the fire season northwards," said Laurence Rouil, director of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service. Larger fires produce more smoke and inject it higher into the atmosphere, allowing it to travel much further, he said. That means countries that experience relatively few wildfires could be increasingly affected by smoke traveling long distances. European wildfires haven been called "completely unprecedented" this summer In the UK, meanwhile, the prolonged dry spell is increasing pressure on already-stretched water supplies. England and Wales recorded their driest July since records began 190 years ago, according to the Met Office, while large parts of England and all of Wales have already been officially declared in drought. The Environment Agency has warned that more areas of England could be declared in drought if dry conditions persist. Weather that was once considered extreme is becoming the "new normal", according to the latest Met Office report on the UK's climate. Its latest assessment found that the hottest day of the year in southern England is now 4.5C warmer than it was between 1961 and 1990. "We are right now living in a time of historic and unprecedented change," said Mike Kendon, Met Office climate information scientist, adding that "evidence shows the climate of the 20th century has now gone". Scientists say El Niño may temporarily push global temperatures even higher. Its effects are being felt against a backdrop of man-made warming, particularly the burning of fossil fuels. The world is now about 1.4C warmer on average than it was in the late 19th Century. title: Pakistan's Zubair seals Tekken 8 Esports World Cup crown
description: Pakistan's Khawaja Muhammad Zubair has claimed the Tekken 8 crown at the Esports World Cup 2026, defeating South Korea's LowHigh in a dominant 5-0 victory in the grand final in Paris.The Tekken 8 competition was held from 5...
content: Published August 09, 2026 Pakistan’s Khawaja Muhammad Zubair has claimed the Tekken 8 crown at the Esports World Cup 2026, defeating South Korea’s LowHigh in a dominant 5-0 victory in the grand final in Paris. The Tekken 8 competition was held from 5 to 8 August, with 32 players competing for a share of the prize pool. Zubair finished the tournament as champion, earning $300,000 in prize money and 1,000 Club Championship points. Zubair defeated LowHigh, one of the established names in the international Tekken scene, in a dominant grand-final performance. The Pakistani player did not drop a single game in the deciding match, completing a 5–0 victory to secure the biggest title of his career. His triumph was particularly remarkable given his relatively limited experience on the international stage. According to the Esports World Cup, Zubair made his international debut just two months before the tournament, when he was eliminated in the pools. He returned to Paris for the Last Chance Qualifier, where he fought his way back into contention before going on to claim the Tekken 8 title. He subsequently battled through the EWC qualification route before defeating several high-profile opponents during his title-winning campaign. His run included a crucial victory over fellow Pakistani star Arslan Ash, while Australia’s Yagami finished third and Ash placed fourth. Zubair topped the final standings ahead of South Korea’s LowHigh, with Yagami in third and Arslan Ash fourth. LowHigh received $130,000 in prize money, while Yagami earned $70,000 and Arslan Ash took home $50,000. Zubair’s achievement adds another significant chapter to Pakistan’s growing reputation in competitive Tekken. The country has established itself as a powerhouse in the fighting game, with players such as Arslan Ash and Atif Butt already recognised internationally. The victory is significant not only for the prize money but also for the manner in which Zubair reached the top. After securing his place in the EWC through the qualification route, the Pakistani player overcame experienced international opposition before producing a commanding performance against LowHigh in the final. The official Tekken esports database lists the champion as Khawaja Muhammad Zubair, who competes under the name AG M. Zubair. His 2026 season record also includes participation in the Tekken World Tour, further strengthening his credentials on the international competitive scene. Copyright © 2026. Geo Television Network. title: Democrats reshape their 2028 presidential race with new primary schedule | CNN Politics
description: The new calendar for the 2028 primaries that Democrats finalized on Saturday will dramatically shake up the race for the party’s next presidential nomination.
content: The new calendar for the 2028 primaries that Democrats finalized on Saturday will dramatically shake up the race for the party’s next presidential nomination. On the last day of its annual summer meeting, the Democratic National Committee approved a primary schedule that replaces Iowa and New Hampshire, the small and preponderantly white states that held the first contests for nearly 50 years, with two racially diverse battlegrounds: South Carolina and Nevada. Under the new calendar , South Carolina, in late January 2028, and Nevada, in early February, will kick off the race for the party’s next presidential nomination. New Hampshire, New Mexico, and then Michigan and Virginia will hold the other early contests through February 2028 before the remaining states start voting in March. Democrats are adopting this new calendar at a time when their progressive and centrist wings are wrestling for control of the party’s direction this year through the greatest concentration of hard-fought primaries in the party’s modern history. All these battles between left and center offer a clear signal that Democrats will face a monumental internal competition for the biggest prize: the party’s 2028 presidential nod . The revised calendar adds an unpredictable new dimension to that struggle. Strategists from all factions in the party believe the new schedule provides plausible pathways to the nomination both for progressive and centrist candidates. But, like a brand new golf course or baseball stadium, no one can predict exactly how this map will play until the candidates begin to compete on it in the 2028 race. “The sequence of primaries and caucuses is one of the most important strategic elements of the nominating process,” says Tad Devine, who has served as a senior strategist for Democratic presidential candidates from Michael Dukakis to Bernie Sanders. “You have to understand the sequence of how these states relate to each other and how you can build momentum by it.” Fiddling with the rules for their presidential nominating process is something between a hobby and a compulsion for Democrats. The party substantially rewrote its nomination rules after the primary contests in 1968, 1980, 1984, 2004 and 2016. But amid all that tinkering with the rules of the primaries, their order remained remarkably stable. Democrats decisively shifted the power to pick their nominees away from party bosses toward voters through caucuses and primaries in 1972. From then through 2020, the party’s nominating process always began with the Iowa caucuses, followed by the New Hampshire primary, whose state law requires it to hold the first primary. Over that nearly half-century, George McGovern in 1972, Bill Clinton in 1992 and Joe Biden in 2020 were the only nominees who did not win either of them — and Biden was the sole victor who did not finish at least second in one. After the 2004 election, amid widespread frustration that Iowa and New Hampshire still wielded so much power in a diversifying party, Democrats chose Nevada and South Carolina to also vote before Super Tuesday. That shift somewhat changed the dynamic of the nominating fights. As the final state to vote before Super Tuesday, South Carolina and its large Black population proved especially influential: The winner there won the nominations in 2008 (Barack Obama), 2016 (Hillary Clinton) and 2020 (Joe Biden). But many Democrats still chafed at the outsized influence of Iowa and New Hampshire in winnowing the field. Not feeling much loyalty to either after his poor showings in 2020 (and Iowa’s botched handling of the vote-counting that year), Biden imposed a calendar for 2024 that created the party’s biggest reshuffle since the primary era began: South Carolina first, followed by Nevada, New Hampshire and Michigan. But the new calendar didn’t get a real test that year as Biden didn’t face a competitive primary.(Democrats were forced to invalidate New Hampshire in 2024 after state officials, following state law, scheduled its primary before South Carolina — a problem that may recur in 2028.) The calendar approved last month by the DNC’s Rules and Bylaws Committee — which the full DNC affirmed Saturday at its meeting in Austin — generally followed the 2024 blueprint, but inserted New Mexico after New Hampshire and Virginia after Michigan. At a time when the DNC and its chair, Ken Martin, have been under fire on several fronts , the new calendar has drawn high marks across the party. The calendar blends large and small states; states with a large Black population (South Carolina, Michigan and Virginia); a large Latino cohort (Nevada and New Mexico); and a strong union presence (Nevada and Michigan), and it includes contests in the DNC’s four national regions. “I’m not here to win a primary election, and neither are our candidates running for president,” Martin said in an interview. “What’s most important is whoever comes out from (the process), from whatever wing of the party they represent, they have to be ready for the general election. And battle-testing them with all parts of our coalition and all parts of the country … prepares whoever comes out to actually win.” As Democratic strategists game out the implications of the new calendar, one question looms largest: At a time when left and center are dueling in so many fierce primaries, does this calendar provide an inherent advantage to either side? Most strategists believe it does not. “I think every candidate from the progressive end of the spectrum, to a moderate, to an establishment person can probably chart a path that they feel OK about,” says Dan Kanninen, the battleground state director for both the Biden and Kamala Harris campaigns in 2024. Jesse Lehrich, a Democratic consultant who publishes an online newsletter and podcast about the 2028 Democratic presidential race, also believes the new schedule offers a pathway for either wing. “I think it’s fair for the left and the center,” he says. “You have more conservative and more progressive states, you have the more diverse and less diverse electorates.” Likewise, Adam Carlson, a Democratic pollster who often works for the progressive wing, says the calendar “is pretty good” for potential leftist candidates. “Honestly, it could have been a lot worse for the left than it ended up being,” Carlson said. For the relatively centrist White candidates — a group that potentially includes Govs. Josh Shapiro, Gavin Newsom and Andy Beshear, Sens. Mark Kelly and Jon Ossoff, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel — South Carolina and Virginia loom as the most important early opportunities. In the 2020 primaries, according to the exit polls , about half of Democratic voters in both states identified as moderate or conservative, far more than in the other four early contests. Black and college-educated White voters, in particular, were more likely to identify as moderate or conservative in those two states than the other four. South Carolina’s Black voters in 2020 famously resurrected Biden’s flatlining candidacy after his early stumbles, and according to the exit polls , only about 15% of them in both 2016 and 2020 backed Sen. Bernie Sanders — whose populist campaign will likely provide the prototype for any of the left-wing candidates in 2028. “We’re not going to be … held to a litmus test” of far-left positions, says Bakari Sellers, a South Carolina-based Democratic activist and CNN political commentator. The complication for the White centrists is that South Carolina’s Black voters — who made up about three-fifths of the electorate there in 2020 — may be drawn to a viable Black contender, whether they are identified with the center or not. Analysts agree that former Vice President Kamala Harris would start with a significant base there, and the state’s movement to the front of the line could encourage her to run. Lehrich reflected many strategists’ war-gaming of the 2028 race when he recently wrote in his newsletter , “The new order is a coup for Harris — the kind that might persuade her to run.” South Carolina’s move to leadoff could also encourage another Black candidate — particularly Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and/or Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock — to run, especially if Harris does not. As the final state to vote before Super Tuesday, Virginia is stepping into the role that had elevated South Carolina. Your midterms questions answered Virginia Democrats have usually favored moderates, not only in presidential primaries (soundly rejecting Sanders for Clinton and Biden), but also in state elections, with candidates such as Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Sens. Mark Warner and Tim Kaine. “That’s quite a triumvirate,” says Larry Sabato, director of the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia. “They may all work together to try to help Democrats to get a nominee who can win in November.” Many Democrats believe the states between South Carolina and Virginia will generally favor potential candidates on the left, such as Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ro Khanna or Sens. Chris Van Hollen and Chris Murphy. Carlson says that with Nevada, New Hampshire and New Mexico lined up in the middle stage of the early window, “It’s pretty easy to imagine” a left candidate “sweeping all three, or two of the three races, after South Carolina.” That, he adds, would allow a left champion to go into Michigan and Virginia “with some real momentum.” Dave Jacobson, a Democratic consultant who has worked extensively in New Mexico, agrees the state, while not culturally liberal, will likely prove receptive to candidates offering a Sanders-style economic message. “New Mexico is one of the poorest states,” Jacobson says. “Democrats who are campaigning on a progressive economic populist message of affordability, health care, education are resonating with Democratic primary voters.” But others say it’s premature to assume Nevada and New Hampshire (if it doesn’t invalidate itself by trying to go first) will also bend left. Sanders won Nevada in 2020, and more voters there (31%) identified as “very liberal” than in the other five early states. But that was for a caucus. In 2028, Nevada will hold a primary, and the expectation that larger electorate will favor the far left “is wishful thinking by some folks,” says Ted Pappageorge, the secretary-treasurer of the Culinary Workers Union, the state’s most powerful political force. For instance, the culinary union, which represents service workers in the casinos, has long opposed the Medicare for All single-payer healthcare proposal that any left-leaning candidate is likely to stress in 2028 . Instead, Pappageorge says, moving Nevada forward to the second contest will pressure candidates to provide practical answers to the daily needs of economically precarious working-class voters who were never as central in Iowa or New Hampshire. “To be No. 2 in the nation,” he says, will allow Nevada to elevate the concerns and experiences of “all workers in this country.” Sanders did win New Hampshire in 2016 and 2020, but in that latter race the most moderate alternatives (Buttigieg, Biden and Sen. Amy Klobuchar) combined for just over half of the vote. New Hampshire’s large constituency of college-educated White voters could break left (as they have in multiple Democratic primaries this year), but in the past many of them have also flocked to cool, brainy centrists such as Gary Hart, Bill Bradley and Buttigieg. Of all the states on the early 2028 calendar, Michigan looks most closely balanced between left and center — as it demonstrated again last week in the acrimonious Senate primary won by about 15,000 votes by progressive Abdul El-Sayed over centrist Rep. Haley Stevens . That echoed Sanders’ razor-thin victory there over Clinton in 2016; on the other hand, Biden decisively beat Sanders in Michigan in 2020. With large populations of Black voters and Whites with and without a college education, Michigan could provide the best test among the early states about which contender can build the broadest coalition within the party —and potentially in November. Kanninen points out that Michigan and Virginia will test the candidates in another new way, because they are much more populous than any of the previous early states. While a candidate can win smaller early states by dominating just one or two voting blocs, he says, these larger and more complex states will demand more. “Once you get to Michigan and Virginia, I think you’ve got to be a five-tool player to be serious,” he said, using a baseball analogy about a player with many skills. Only candidates with “a frame durable enough” to attract “all the disparate parts of the Democratic coalition” are likely to do well in those two states, he says. If there is a master key to this new calendar, it may be that it will reward a candidate who can appeal to both Black voters (a big presence in half the early states) and college-educated White voters (who are very likely to outnumber blue-collar Whites in all of them except New Mexico and maybe Michigan). Historically it hasn’t been easy for one candidate to marry those two constituencies, since Black voters often gravitate toward grounded bread-and-butter options (like Bill and Hillary Clinton or Biden) while well-educated Whites are often drawn to more ideological or idealistic alternatives (think Sanders or Gary Hart). The one modern candidate who did run well with both groups was Obama in 2008, and the states he relied on to beat Hillary Clinton in their epic primary duel may offer the clearest map to success on this new course. Then again, as Sabato points out, the rules and calendar changes Democrats have instituted over the years have rarely worked out exactly as planned. “When you try to structure a selection process to produce a certain result, especially in this party,” Sabato says, “in all likelihood, you are going to be disappointed.” Still, however it unfolds in 2028, the new schedule represents the biggest reordering of the Democratic nominating calendar in over half a century — and the beginning of a new era for the party. title: More hosepipe bans in force as drought declared - is your area affected? - BBC News
description: Nearly 30 million people have been placed under hosepipe bans due to higher demand and low rainfall.
content: Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales are under drought conditions, with repeated heatwaves leaving water supplies under strain. Both England and Wales provisionally recorded their driest July on record. This lack of rainfall - on top of hot, dry weather in spring and early summer - has begun to take its toll on rivers, crops and nature. Wessex Water has become the latest water provider to announce a hosepipe ban - the company's first for 50 years - taking the total number of people under such a measure to nearly 30 million. So how is your area doing and are you in a drought? There is no single definition of drought, but it is characterised by a period of low rainfall. As the ground dries out, crops and vegetation can begin to struggle. If dry conditions persist, rivers, reservoirs and groundwater levels can also fall, putting pressure on water supplies. Environmental bodies in each UK nation decide whether to declare drought or water scarcity by assessing current water resources alongside weather forecasts. Both drought and water scarcity can lead to hosepipe bans, if they are not already in place. While drought is driven by prolonged dry weather, water scarcity occurs when demand for water outstrips the available supply. This summer, restrictions have been introduced in some areas to help manage high demand. But while recent months have seen temperatures regularly exceed 35C, winter was much wetter than usual. It has raised questions about how effectively water resources are being managed, and whether the UK is prepared for the drier summers expected with climate change. So far, ten UK water companies have announced hosepipe bans. This means hosepipes cannot be used for watering gardens, washing vehicles and windows, and filling pools. Nine companies are spread across central, southern and eastern parts of England, and one is in Wales. In England, nearly three-quarters of the country is now in drought, according to the Environment Agency (EA). Northern parts of England are in "prolonged dry weather" - the category below drought. Elsewhere, the whole of Wales is in drought, with Natural Resources Wales saying sustained high temperatures were causing the condition of the natural environment to "deteriorate". There are no official droughts currently in Northern Ireland. Scotland does not declare droughts but monitors "water scarcity". While conditions have improved in some parts of Scotland following recent rainfall, some eastern areas remain in the two most extreme categories of "moderate" or "significant" scarcity, according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency. Our three main sources of water are rivers, reservoirs and from deep underground. Almost all river flows in England and Wales were classed as "below normal", "notably low" or "exceptionally low" in July, according to the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH). "This is the third time in the last five years that drought conditions have intensified rapidly following exceptional spring and summer dryness," said Steve Turner, a hydrologist at the UKCEH. He added that low river flows are likely to persist well into the autumn. England's reservoirs are some way below average levels for the time of year. Wales' reservoirs are also declining, but Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water has said its water resource position is "relatively strong". Reservoir levels in Northern Ireland and Scotland are close to average, according to the latest available data. South-east England relies more heavily on groundwater than reservoirs. Groundwater originates as rainfall and is naturally stored beneath the surface in the pore spaces and fractures in rocks. Groundwater levels are generally declining following the prolonged dry weather, but almost half of monitored groundwater sites recorded levels considered "normal" or higher in July. Water can flow more slowly through some rock types than others, sometimes taking years to fully respond to current conditions. These groundwater stores "respond more slowly to changes in the climate than rivers, which is why they provide a useful buffer during periods of drought", said Prof Alan MacDonald of the British Geological Survey. It is why groundwater droughts in the south of England generally take a longer time to develop but can be longer-lasting if they do occur. Droughts are complex phenomena, driven by a mix of natural and human causes. The Met Office expects the UK to experience drier summers on average in future as the world warms, though there has been no clear trend so far. But rising temperatures can play a more direct role by drawing extra moisture from the soil via evaporation. "A warmer atmosphere is thirstier for moisture and this can mean water in the soil, rivers and reservoirs are depleted more effectively, leading to more rapidly onsetting droughts, heatwaves and wildfires," said Richard Allan, professor of climate science at the University of Reading. But there are other factors that determine whether dry conditions lead to water shortages, including how we use water. In a landmark review into the water sector of England and Wales, water companies were criticised for historic underinvestment in water infrastructure. As part of plans to address water shortages, the government and water companies are planning nine new reservoirs for England by 2050 , in addition to one under construction at Havant Thicket in Hampshire. But the EA has warned that measures to tackle water leaks and control water demand - potentially including hosepipe bans - may be needed in England too . Water companies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland - which are all public bodies or non-profit - also said they were taking steps to secure future supplies. title: Zimbabwe ferry disaster: 72 dead, including 18 children | CNN
description: Eighteen children were among more than 70 people killed when an overloaded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe this week, police said Saturday after rescuers recovered more bodies.
content: Eighteen children were among more than 70 people killed when an overloaded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe this week, police said Saturday after rescuers recovered more bodies. The ferry capsized in strong waves on Tuesday. Police said that 26 more bodies had been recovered since then, bringing the death toll to 72. The aging ferry was traveling from the town of Kariba to rural and fishing communities in the country’s northwest, where roads are damaged and public transportation is scarce. Authorities have not said how many people were aboard or how many remain missing. Estimates have put the number of passengers as high as 153, while authorities say the ferry’s capacity is 90. Zimbabwe’s disaster management agency has said 77 people were rescued. Authorities initially said the number of children aboard was unknown because those below ticketing age were not included in passenger estimates. A police list released later showed that 16 of the child victims were aged 10 or younger, with the youngest just 1. Kariba is the world’s largest human-made lake by volume, created by damming the mighty Zambezi River in the late 1950s and early 1960s. It stretches more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) and is up to 40 kilometers (25 miles) wide in places. Zimbabwe and Zambia share the lake, with their border running through its middle. © 2026 Cable News Network. A Warner Bros. Discovery Company. All Rights Reserved. title: Democrat 2028 calendar elevates states with Black, Latino voters | CNN Politics
description: Democrats on Saturday finalized their 2028 presidential primary schedule, targeting diverse populations that will help shape the party’s fight for White House seat.
content: Democrats on Saturday adopted a 2028 presidential primary schedule that moves states with sought-after diverse populations to the front of a calendar that will shape their party’s fight to win the White House. Democratic National Committee members gave final approval to six early voting states, with South Carolina, which has a substantial Black population, continuing to kick off the party’s nominating contests on January 22, 2028. Nevada, a western presidential battleground, will follow on February 1. The four other early voting states are New Hampshire on February 8, New Mexico on February 15, Michigan on February 22 and Virginia on February 29. The calendar excludes Iowa, a traditional bellwether state for candidates, from the early lineup. In choosing to include Nevada and New Mexico in the early contests, the party has frontloaded the calendar with states that have large contingents of Latino voters, a group that President Donald Trump made inroads with during the 2024 presidential election. In an interview with CNN, DNC Chair Ken Martin hailed the calendar as “the most diverse” in the party’s history. “It’s going to battle-test our nominee with key parts of our coalition and key parts of the country in a way that we’ve never seen before,” he said. The vote, on the final day of the DNC’s summer meeting, comes amid a midterm primary election season that has seen Democratic voters swing between progressive insurgents and moderate candidates — an internal struggle over the party’s direction that likely will loom over the crowded race for the White House. Martin, who has faced criticism of his leadership of the DNC and stewardship of its finances, insisted that those ideological differences should not divide Democrats as they barrel toward this November’s high-stakes midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. “We are a big tent party,” the party chief told a gathering of the DNC women’s caucus on the opening day of the meeting Thursday. “And as long as I’m the chair, we’re going to continue to be.” “Everybody is welcomed in this party,” Martin said to strong applause and hoots of approval from those assembled in a ballroom at a Hilton hotel in downtown Austin. Before the vote, party officials from Iowa — which has long held the first nominating contest — made known their displeasure with the new calendar. “We need a Midwest and a truly rural state to be among the first four states if we hope to build sustainable and lasting majorities that enact real and meaningful change,” Iowa Democratic Party Chair Rita Hart argued, urging DNC members to reject the calendar. In the end, the new schedule passed on a voice vote, prompting sustained applause from the DNC crowd. In addition to keeping Iowa out of the early state lineup, the committee members pushed New Hampshire deeper into the calendar, though that could also cause some internal party tensions. New Hampshire law requires the state’s top election official to schedule a primary at least seven days before another state carries out a primary. Proponents of the new schedule say the calendar shake-up will help Democrats engage with the voters the party needs to win the presidential election. Nevada and Michigan both have large amounts of union members, and have substantial numbers of Black voters. And New Mexico’s inclusion puts a heavily Latino and rural border state into the mix. “New Mexico looks a lot like the America Democrats need to win,” Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez, a Democrat from the state, told CNN in an interview before the final vote. “When our presidential candidates come and listen to and inspire our Latino voters, Latinos across the country are going to understand that they are not being taken for granted.” The DNC gathering occurred during a time of internal strife for the national party, with some members criticizing Martin’s management decisions and voicing alarm over the national party’s financial health. The DNC has raised $207 million so far in this cycle — compared with nearly $279 million collected by the Republican National Committee, according to Federal Election Commission filings. But the Democratic committee lags far behind its Republican counterpart in available resources less than three months before the midterms. The DNC ended June with $2 million in debt, while the RNC had nearly $129 million remaining in the bank, FEC filings show. Martin defended his record. During an interview with CNN, he pointed to a string of electoral victories for Democrats around the country in recent months as an outgrowth of his decision to invest in a permanent campaign infrastructure. “By every objective measure on how to measure a party — and certainly party leadership — I’m succeeding,” Martin said. Asked about a report in The New York Times that the party has urged vendors to delay sending invoices until after the midterms to help alleviate the cash crunch, Martin told CNN it was “standard practice” to renegotiate vendor contracts “to make sure you can meet cash flow and keep those relationships intact.” Martin, who was elected chair early last year, has defenders in the DNC, including among state party chairs who have benefited from the national party’s new investments in their work. (Last year, the DNC increased the amount it sends to state parties. Blue states began receiving an additional $5,000 a month, for a total of $17,500, and red states got a boost of $10,000 a month, for a total of $22,500.) “There is no appetite for his removal,” Michael Kapp, a DNC member from California, said flatly. “He’s doing exactly what we asked him to do: building up state parties, investing in training and organizing programs, investing in partisan voter registration and not hoarding our cash.” Daniele Monroe-Moreno, who chairs the Nevada Democratic Party, said Martin’s investment strategy is making a difference for Democrats in her state, who hope to flip the governor’s mansion and an open US House seat this fall. “Money’s nice in the bank,” she said, “but I’d rather have the money on the ground doing the organizing.” Over the course of the gathering, top Democrats exhorted members to stay focused on winning races this fall, rather than party infighting. “Nobody sitting in Danville, Virginia, right now at their kitchen table worrying about paying their heating bills or groceries is worried about what’s going on at the DNC headquarters, I promise you all that,” former Virginia Gov. Terry McAuliffe, who has also been a DNC chairman, told the gathering on Saturday. “We need to be unified,” McAuliffe said. This story has been updated with additional information. title: Selena Gomez and her mental health startup accused of fraud | CNN Business
description: Several investors in Selena Gomez’s mental health startup Wondermind sued the popstar Thursday, claiming they were misled about the startup’s success and her involvement in it.
content: Markets Hot Stocks Fear & Greed Index Latest Market News Hot Stocks Several investors in Selena Gomez’s mental health startup Wondermind sued the popstar Thursday, claiming they were misled about the startup’s success and her involvement in it. Wondermind launched in 2021, with Gomez listed as co-founder, “chief impact officer,” and head of marketing, according to the suit. The media platform was designed to give users “easy, doable ways to put your mental fitness first every day,” its website reads, directing visitors to sign up for a newsletter. Five investors said in the lawsuit that they put in $1.2 million in 2022, expecting Gomez to leverage her star power and massive social media following to build up the company. Instead, “for three years, while the Company quietly collapsed around them, not one of its founders, officers, or directors said a word to the investors whose money was funding the collapse,” the lawsuit alleged. “The allegations that Selena Gomez engaged in any way whatsoever in any purported ‘fraud’ or other wrongdoing are completely meritless, both factually and legally. We will vigorously defend these false allegations and indeed are filing a motion to dismiss the baseless claims against her,” Gomez’s attorney Mathew Rosengart told CNN in a statement. The investors also sued Mandy Teefey, Gomez’s mother and co-chief executive officer, and their former business partner, Daniella Pierson. The parties are being sued for securities fraud, common law fraud, breach of contract and other claims. The plaintiffs are seeking to recoup their investments as well as damages and attorney fees. The company said it had a $95 million valuation in 2022, when investors were allegedly led to believe there would be corporate partnerships with companies like JPMorgan as well as “advertising deals, celebrity cover stories, and a groundbreaking app,” according to the lawsuit. Selena Gomez launches new media platform with a focus on mental health “The partnerships did not exist. The initiatives never materialized. The app was never built,” the investors alleged. Investors found out about the company’s troubles in an explosive article published by The Cut last year, which reported that the company was burdened by internal power and relationship struggles. The article forms a major basis for the lawsuit. The suit cited The Cut reporting when it said Gomez didn’t fulfill her contractual obligations because of “her long-running personal struggles with her mother.” Gomez, Teefey and Pierson collectively owned almost 90% of the company’s shares, the lawsuit claimed. Teefey told investors that Pierson allegedly used investor funds to help pay her rent in New York City, which came to approximately $60,000 a month, according to the lawsuit. Pierson left Wondermind in 2023. In a statement on Thursday, Pierson said she “denies the allegations against her and welcomes the opportunity to present concrete documentation and financial records that establish the facts.” She also said she never used investor funds for personal expenses. Teefey and Wondermind did not return a request for comment. This story has been updated with additional content. Most stock quote data provided by BATS. title: Eye contact: What to do when there are no clear-cut rules | CNN
description: Eye contact isn’t just about being polite. It’s fundamental to human connection. But there’s no hard and fast rule about how much eye contact is appropriate.
content: “Look at me when I’m talking to you.” It’s a request I heard from my mother throughout much of my childhood, and even into my adult life. Somehow, what has always felt like the right amount of eye contact from my end has often been less than for her. So many of us have been told to look someone in the eye when speaking. But how much eye contact is the appropriate amount when talking or listening to another person? There’s no rule, but almost always “people look more while listening than when speaking, although looking is hardly ever just a steady stare,” said Judith Hall, social psychologist and University Distinguished Professor of Psychology, Emerita at Northeastern University in Boston, in an email. That’s because our eyes are constantly moving around in many small ways when talking or listening. And while people generally have a good sense of when eye contact feels like too much or too little as it’s happening, Hall said quantifying the right amount is not possible. There are, however, some subtleties to consider. A guide to mastering small talk with just about anyone, according to experts It can feel offensive when you’re having a conversation with someone who is averting their gaze. But making eye contact during conversation has functions that go beyond being polite. “Eye contact isn’t just a social courtesy; it’s actually a brain-stimulating interaction, and it’s really fundamental to human connection,” said Melissa J. Perry, dean of the College of Public Health at George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia. As social beings, humans glean information from others by looking, observing and listening, Perry said. She noted that our brains are “optimized” for seeking out sensory input from others through eye contact and other nonverbal cues, including facial expressions and posture. Little kids can likely read your emotions even when you wear a face mask, study finds “Neurobiologically, the brain is responding to the authenticity and empathy and credibility of the person before the mind is forming an opinion about what they’re saying,” Perry added. Eye contact also has neurochemical effects within the body, including the release of oxytocin, the neuropeptide that plays a crucial role in social bonding, said Paula Niedenthal, a professor of psychology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison whose research examines neural, cognitive, social and cultural/societal influences on facial mimicry and eye gaze. “The initial function of eye contact is to create a social bond with somebody and to generate activation in the reward systems of the brain and the production of oxytocin to make sure that everybody’s gotten involved in this dance and is going to stay there,” Niedenthal added. In addition to interacting with the brain’s reward system, eye contact is also important for gathering information. We learn about people’s moods, behavior and many other things by watching them, Hall noted, whether that’s through direct interactions with people or while watching them without their knowledge. Making eye contact with someone when they’re talking to you doesn’t have to mean staring right into their eyes, she said. Even people who don’t have difficulty hearing tend to lip-read some during conversation, Hall said, in case you’ve noticed yourself watching someone’s mouth as they talk. Dogs know if we’re happy, sad or scared just from our expressions, study suggests When it comes to communicating, more eye contact isn’t always better, Perry cautioned. “Healthy communication depends on natural intermittent eye contact,” she said. “Too little can suggest uncertainty or disengagement, while too much can feel intimidating or confrontational.” Averting a gaze during communication can also imply a distance and aloofness, she said, or even a sense of secrecy. People who consider themselves to be in a dominant position compared with the person they’re talking with have somewhat altered ratios when it comes to how much they make eye contact while speaking and listening, Hall said. “Their ratio of looking while speaking goes up and their ratio of looking while listening goes down,” she said. After years of progress on gender, the male gaze is back There are also differences between men and women. Women are “well established to gaze at others in conversation more than men do,” said Hall, with the highest levels of gaze during communication occurring in pairs of females, and the lowest among pairs of males. Cultural differences can also come into play when it comes to what’s considered an acceptable amount of eye contact. “There is a lot of cultural universality although specific cultures can have their own norms,” Hall said. Ethnic groups can vary when it comes to certain situations involving eye contact, too, such as whether sustained eye contact with a superior while talking is considered paying attention or taken as a lack of deference, she said. Life on the spectrum with Mason Niedenthal said there’s a “continuum” when it comes to the extent to which eye contact can feel too arousing to different people — another reason there’s no hard and fast rule when it comes to how much eye contact is appropriate in social settings. People with some neurodevelopmental conditions, such as autism, typically avoid eye contact, Niedenthal said. “The claim is that for those with autism, the high arousal is aversive. Avoidance is thus an adaptive emotion regulation strategy,” she said, noting that it isn’t the only reason why autism is associated with eye contact avoidance. The best online prescription glasses in 2026, tested by editors (Courtesy CNN Underscored) If you’re not comfortable with how much someone is looking at you or vice versa, what do you do? Just being aware of the power of eye contact and other nonverbal forms of communication is a step in the right direction, Perry said. “It’s far more powerful and impactful than any of us recognize,” she said. Terry Ward is a freelance journalist and travel writer based in Tampa, Florida, who pitched this story after asking her husband to look her in the eyes when she spoke to him. title: Antarctica's first ever dinosaur bone discovered in a drawer - BBC News
description: The fossil, collected in Antarctica in 1985, is part of the tail of a beast called a Titanosaur.
content: The fossil was originally found in 1985 on James Ross Island in Antarctica An unassuming-looking fossil that spent 40 years lying forgotten in a drawer has turned out to be the first dinosaur bone ever found in Antarctica. The specimen was unearthed in 1985, but the team that discovered it was not sure what it was - so it was stored away in the geology collection of the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) in Cambridge. Now the fossil has been studied by palaeontologists who have confirmed that it is a tail bone from a type of dinosaur called a Titanosaur - this group contained the largest dinosaurs to ever walk the Earth. The discovery helps to reveal more about how these beasts lived in a part of the world where the fossil record is sparse. The discovery was recorded in geologist Mike Thomson's notebook Dr Mark Evans, the collections manager at BAS, recently spotted the fossil amongst thousands of specimens brought back from expeditions to Antarctica over the decades. "It's only when you start thinking 'what's in this drawer', that sometimes you come across something and you think, 'Ah, this looks interesting'," he said. The specimen was originally collected on James Ross Island and its discovery was recorded in a field notebook kept by geologist Dr Mike Thomson. Alongside a tiny, neat sketch of the fossil dated 9 December 1985 he has written "vertebra of large reptile", noting it was about 10cm wide. Evans says the team that found it probably thought the fossil belonged to a marine reptile. But as soon as he saw it, Evans realised the vertebra looked very dinosaur-like. And the date of its discovery meant it would have been the first dinosaur fossil found on the continent. When Titanosaurs inhabited Antarctica 80 million years ago it would have been covered in lush forest He called in Prof Paul Barrett from the Natural History Museum (NHM) to confirm his discovery. "Although it's not too much to look at, it actually has a really distinctive shape," Barrett told us, holding the fossil in his hands. He pointed to a hollow on one end of the fossil and then turned it over to reveal a rounded bump at the other. The vertebrae line up to create a series of ball-and-socket joints running from head to tail. "As soon as I saw it, I knew what we were dealing withâ¦ it was a dead cert we were dealing with a Titanosaur," he said. "This is a combination of features that's completely unique to these types of dinosaurs." A Titanosaur cast, on loan from the NHM, is on display at Peterborough Cathedral More than 100 species of Titanosaur have now been identified around the world. All are four-legged plant eaters, with very long necks that helped them reach up into trees and long counter-balancing tails. The very biggest Titanosaurs were more than 115ft (35m) long and weighed about 60 tonnes. From the size of this tail bone, the scientists estimate the Antarctic Titanosaur was about 23ft (7m) in length. "Maybe it was a juvenile dinosaur, or maybe it was a genuinely small one - one that was actually bucking the trend for the rest of the group as a smaller adult," explained Barrett. This dinosaur would have lived 82 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous Period when Antarctica was very different from how it is today. It would have been covered in lush forest, providing ample food for the plant-eating beast. Dr Mark Evans spotted the fossil in the British Antarctic Survey's geology collections The long-forgotten fossil now holds an important place in the history of exploration in Antarctica. Other dinosaur fossils have been found in this remote part of the world in the years after 1985 - but not very many. Antarctica is a challenging place for palaeontologists to work and the ice conceals the prehistoric record in the rock beneath. "It shows that an area that we now think is really uninhabitable was once actually very habitable and had this huge cast of characters living on it," explained Barrett. "It's helping us to work out how they fitted into these broader ecosystems at the very bottom of the world about 80 million years ago." AÂ paper on the discovery , external has been published in the journal Acta Palaeontologica Polonica. title: Simpler, older version of Stonehenge found three miles from famous site - BBC News
description: The structure consisted of two posts that lined up with the solstices 5,000 years ago.
content: The huge stones at Stonehenge mark the movements of the Sun Archaeologists believe they have discovered an earlier, much simpler version of Stonehenge about 3 miles (5km) away from the prehistoric monument. All that remains of the older structure is two holes in the ground, but the team says they held wooden posts that lined up with the Sun on the summer and winter solstices - the longest and shortest days of the year - in the same way as Stonehenge. The site has been dated to about 5,000 years old, which predates Stonehenge by 500 years. Artefacts were also found at the site, including pottery, flint tools and animal bone, suggesting prehistoric people held gatherings there. Phil Harding, from Wessex Archaeology, who led the excavation, said it was one of the best finds of his long career. "Two post pits tell me more about the people 5,000 years ago," he said. "This tells me about the whole community, this tells me about how they were thinking, how they were behaving, how they were revering the heavens." Phil Harding says discovering the structure has been a career high The huge stones at Stonehenge are precisely placed to line up with the Sun. If you stand in middle of the circle at sunrise on the summer solstice, you will see the Sun come up over a stone called the heel stone to the north east of the circle. On midwinter, if standing in the centre of the circle, you would see the sun set over an altar stone to the south west of the site. The structure, discovered in the village of Bulford, was a much more simple construction made up of just two wooden posts, which have long since rotted away. They were positioned 120m (394ft) apart and estimated to be between 2m and 4m high. When Harding uncovered the intriguing holes, he noticed that they seemed to line up with the Sun, just like Stonehenge located a few miles away. "I got my pencil and ruler, and I joined them up, and I was aware that they were kind of pointing in the general direction of the sunrise on midsummer," he said. A number of artefacts were found at the site, including this rounded flint knife Dating of items like this carved bone show the site is 5,000 years old Fine pottery found at Bulford suggests people were coming there to feast 1 of 3 The traces of the earlier structure were found a decade ago in Bulford when the ground was cleared for new army housing. But it is only now that a detailed analysis of the alignment has been carried out, which involved turning back the celestial clock. "The sky - the positions of the Sun, Moon, planets and stars - they change very slowly throughout the centuries. We don't really notice it during our lifetimes," said Dr Fabio Silva, an archaeoastronomer from Bournemouth University and the Skyscape Academy. "So we basically need to reconstruct the sky, what it looked like exactly 5,000 years ago, where the Sun was rising and what time it was rising in those places. "If you take into account the width of the posts… then the alignment is exactly, exactly right. It's accurately aligned to summer solstice sunrise and winter solstice sunset." The pits that held these posts were not the only discovery during the excavation, surrounding them were dozens of other holes containing artefacts belonging to the prehistoric people of Bulford village. These objects have helped to establish the age of the site. The team used radiocarbon dating, which looks at how a special form of carbon changes over time, to work out that the structure was 5,000 years old. The artefacts included an antler that would have been used for digging, and other carved animal bones, as well as finely decorated fragments of pottery. Tools made of flint were also uncovered, including a rare Neolithic knife that has been rounded into a disc-shape (discoidal). "It was, I think, our star find," said Harding of Wessex Archaeology. "What is so special about it is the workmanship that's gone into it. That is the work of real craftsmanship." He said the knife was found in an upright position, like it had been carefully placed, and he wonders if it had a symbolic significance. "Maybe that discoidal shape is some sort of reference to the Sun, who knows?," he said. Each hole was about half a metre wide and the two were separated by 120m (400ft) The monument at Bulford dates to the same time as the earliest phase of activity at Stonehenge, when the first earthworks were built half a Millennium before the stones were placed. "The discovery of Bulford actually suggests that maybe the people who built the first stages of Stonehenge were based or living there, or at least gathering seasonally to do the construction work at Stonehenge," said Dr Jennifer Wexler, curator of history at English Heritage. But why were these prehistoric people so fascinated with the Sun? "The people who built Stonehenge and the people who were at Bulford were early farmers, and their livelihoods really were connected to the seasons and the Sun doing its job," explained Wexler. Today, the summer solstice at Stonehenge is the biggest draw, when thousands of people come to witness sunrise at the monument. But Wexler says 5,000 years ago, the winter solstice - the shortest day of the year -held more significance for the ancient communities. "Winter might have been particularly important because it's a time of year when the light is literally dying, and maybe you need to do something to evoke that return or mark it, because then it's a return of the spring, when hopefully your crops and your animals will thrive." title: Colombia’s earthquake tore apart this family with triplets. Only one survived | CNN
description: Ana María Saavedra Caycedo lay under the rubble for hours reeling from arm injuries and a fractured pelvis. When she was finally pulled out, it was into a harsh new reality: one where she was the sole survivor of her immediate family.
content: Lee el artículo en español Ana María Saavedra Caycedo lay under the rubble for hours reeling from arm injuries and a fractured pelvis. When she was finally pulled out, it was into a harsh new reality: one where she was the sole survivor of her immediate family. When the 7.4 magnitude earthquake shook western Colombia on August 10, the Saavedra Caycedo family was in their apartment in Cali, one of the hardest-hit cities. Search and rescue efforts at the site began immediately and continued for days. Family and friends took to the streets to ask for help and volunteer in the rescue operations. The triplets, Ana Maria, Sofia and Isabella Saavedra Caycedo; their father Jair Saavedra; their mother Vicky Caycedo and their uncle Diego Caycedo would all be pulled from the debris in the hours and days that followed. Satellite images show devastation of Colombia earthquake The parents were found embracing in their final moments. Sofia and Diego were found dead too. And Isabella’s body was the last to be pulled from the rubble, the triplets’ cousin Camila Martínez Sierra said. A family-organized GoFundMe campaign for Ana Maria has already received thousands of donations. The campaign page says she has already undergone surgery “and now faces a long recovery process.” “Our hearts are broken by the loss of my uncle Jairo and Vicky and my cousins Sofía and Isabella,” Marinez Sierra posted to Instagram on Friday. “Now is the time to stay united and be there for our cousin Ana. Every bit of help, prayer, donation, and sharing counts.” The triplets, according to the family’s fundraising campaign, had recently graduated from university and worked together. “They had dreams, plans, and a whole life ahead of them,” their family wrote on the GoFundMe page. “We want Ana María to have a solid foundation to recover physically and emotionally and to restart her life, without also having to worry about how to pay for everything that is to come.” Martínez Sierra remembered her relatives with several photos and videos of large family gatherings, trips, parties and moments they shared together. One photo shows the family dressed in matching white outfits and black hats, sitting poolside with wide smiles at what appears to be a family reunion. Another shows them gathered around a night-time bonfire. “I can only look at these videos and photos with a heart full of memories and a mix of love, nostalgia, and a pain I still don’t know how to explain,” she wrote in an Instagram post. “Here are our reunions, the laughter, the hugs, the family moments, my uncles, the triplets … moments we lived without imagining that one day we would look at these images in such a different way,” Martínez Sierra said. The Saavedra Caycedo family are among the at least 294 people confirmed to have been killed. Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management said another 320 are missing while nearly 4,000 were injured in the earthquake. More than 12,000 homes have been destroyed and over 100 buildings have been leveled. The earthquake was the deadliest to hit Colombia in decades . Families have been sharing urgent pleas on social media, hoping to track down missing loved ones and rescuers are continuing to work through the rubble. “One never thinks that a photo can become such a precious memory, nor that a hug that seemed so ordinary could become something we would keep forever in our hearts,” Martínez Sierra said. “This earthquake changed our lives in a matter of seconds,” Martínez Sierra said. “It reminded us, in the most painful way, that nothing is guaranteed and that many times we put off a hug, a phone call, an ‘I love you,’ a meeting, a visit.” © 2026 Cable News Network. title: How the UK's extreme heat is shifting the conversation about air-con - BBC News
description: Should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences?
content: How the UK's extreme heat is shifting the conversation about air-con Mandy Bourne lives with her 80-year-old mum in a top-floor social housing flat in the West Midlands. Both struggle with health conditions exacerbated by the recent heatwaves. For Mandy, temperature shifts can trigger flare-ups of her chronic lung condition. "I've got COPD and sometimes I can't breathe," she explains. Across the UK, solid brick homes like theirs quietly absorb heat the way they have for decades. Charged-up walls radiate warmth back into rooms that never get the chance to cool. Mandy says she is constantly reaching for her inhaler as her flat overheats. "It's red hot in the flat. The sun is just beaming in." Many homes are built to radiate warmth back into rooms That retained warmth can push night-time temperatures in urban centres up to 7C higher than the surrounding countryside. This is the urban heat island effect and it is at its most dangerous in the early hours when bodies need cooler air and cannot find it. Modelling of a previous West Midlands heatwave by researchers from the University of Birmingham reached the bleak conclusion that the heat island impact alone accounted for roughly half the 130 heat-related deaths. Jo Shields, head of sustainability for Mandy's housing association Walsall Housing Group, known as whg - which owns 23,000 homes across Walsall and the Midlands - hears the same complaint time and again. "The heat gain stays within the concrete or the brick," she says, "so the night-time cooling becomes harder". Last summer, as the region baked, the residents of Ellum Pointe - a whg scheme for the over-55s - began telling their landlords they simply could not cool their flats. The response was improvised. "We took the community room, closed all the windows and doors, and we put a mobile air-conditioning unit in there," Shields says. "And basically, we created an internal cool room." She likens it to the warm spaces opened during the pandemic for people who couldn't afford to heat their homes. Shields' job has previously focused on decarbonising - reducing the emissions from the housing stock - but she now has to balance those pressures with the need to adapt homes to rising heat. Across the country, landlords are facing similar choices. As Britain enters a new kind of summer, with homes built to trap warmth and heatwaves intensifying, two questions loom: should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences, and how much should we spend on adapting homes versus cutting carbon? For 40 years, wealthy countries have focused heavily on cutting the carbon emissions that cause climate change, known as mitigation. Adaptation such as designing housing so it is more resilient to hotter temperatures and installing air conditioning has not always had the same focus. Reducing emissions was seen as morally right because richer nations produced most of the gases that have warmed the planet. And with that focus came a funding imbalance. In 2023, $1.8tn was given to mitigation, while adaptation did not secure even 5% of that – it scraped $65bn globally. Spending too much on adaption was seen by many as giving up on the fight against climate change. But this mainstream view has now been challenged. In a memo published last year, Bill Gates - a man who has poured billions into clean technology - argued that the climate movement's "doomsday" fixation on temperature targets had diverted money from the things that most improve lives in a warming world. Climate change is serious, he wrote, but "will not lead to humanity's demise". Governments, he added, should be investing in cooling for the countries that need it. The publication sparked backlash from climate scientists who accused Gates of making arguments based on "false dichotomies" - pitting mitigation and adaptation against each other. Some, including US President Donald Trump, saw it as sign that the billionaire was "finally" supporting the belief that climate change was a hoax. Gates insisted he was not arguing against cutting emissions, but rather for spending money where it saves the most suffering. The row that followed exposed the real fault line that's coming to the surface this summer: not whether to cut carbon or adapt to the heat – but how much to spend on each. There's another reason that muddies the waters and helps explain why cutting carbon became the prime focus – it was investable. Heat pumps and EVs can be sold. Spending on shade, ventilation and cooler hospitals and homes all produce little in the way of bankable returns - even if it reduces costs of climate change long term. Baroness Brown - also known as the engineer Julia King, who chairs the adaptation committee of the government's Climate Change Committee - argues this imbalance is written into UK law. Under the Climate Change Act, the mitigation half of her committee recommends legally binding carbon budgets that ministers must deliver and are marked on every year. Adaptation has no such teeth: the government writes its own risk assessment and its own plans. "Essentially, the government writes an essay, and our job is to say, is it doing the things it said would do in its essay. It's not actually to say, are these things any good." Her committee has spent, she says, "almost 20 years pulling our hair out" - but this year has been different. With exquisite timing it produced a report just as the first heatwave was striking Britain in May - urging lawmakers to set hard adaptation targets. "We've actually looked at the difference that providing some sort of support with cooling for the 30% of most vulnerable homes, and cooling in our hospitals, [with] preventive care visits. The modelling we've done suggests that that would reduce 40% of the increase in heat-related deaths that are predicted for 2050." "We're saying these are the actions that can make a big difference." One of the most controversial ideas in the report is on air conditioning. Right now, only 5% or so of English homes have a cooling unit. The Committee recommends fitting these devices in hospitals and care homes within 10 years, and schools in 25 years. This goes against years of government advice that passive cooling was the preferred method - using shade, ventilation and other design features to bring down temperatures, not mechanical means. Prof Mat Santamouris from the University of New South Wales, is the world's most-cited researcher on urban overheating. Machines, he argues, should be the last line of defence: reflective roofing alone, in one of his studies, dragged indoor temperatures from around 43C towards 30C, while a ceiling fan gives comfort for a fraction of the cost. Putting up unshaded glass towers in cities, he says, is "crazy". "We cannot air-condition our way out of climate change." Santamouris is scathing about who is driving the air con demand - the industry, he says, is "extremely powerful" – adding that passive cooling adds its own economic growth, as money is spent on plumbers and builders. "We cannot air-condition our way out of climate change," says Prof Santamouris Against him stand those who think Britain's hostility to cooling has curdled into a type of masochism. David Lawrence, of the Centre for British Progress think tank, puts it plainly: we don't tell people to insulate their homes in winter and then skip the radiators. So why insist shade and shutters are enough in summer? He points out that air conditioning is standard now in offices, hotels and shops, "but we don't expect it for schools and hospitals - which is kind of odd, because those are places where millions of people are every day", and where heat measurably dents concentration, learning and health. This dispute over the pros and cons of the technology is becoming political. Some London councils, following a planning "cooling hierarchy", say low-energy ways of keeping homes cool should be prioritised over air conditioning and in a small number of cases have ordered property owners to remove them; the Conservative front bench calls it "dark ages" miserabilism; other MPs and political commentators demand an "air-con revolution". Since April, in England and Wales the Boiler Upgrade Scheme has offered £2,500 towards a reversible air-air heat pump: a machine that warms a home in winter and cools it in summer. It is, in all but name, Britain's first air-conditioning subsidy - but it is badged as a heat pump, and only worth a third of the £7,500 for a heating-only model. Such has been the silence around this grant, that in its first month only around 45 households claimed it. By comparison, the numbers claiming a heating-only model ran into the thousands. In Scotland homeowners can also get a £7,500 grant for a heat pump via its Home Energy scheme - but for air-air versions that could offer cooling there is no funding at all. And in Northern Ireland there is no universal heat pump grant offered for households. Under the terms of the England and Wales scheme, some people cannot apply at all. It is closed to social housing and new builds - which many argue shuts out the very people most exposed. Take Woolwich, in south-east London, where a resident called Keisha says her top-floor flat reaches 43C in a heatwave. She calls the building "inhumane"; she and around twenty neighbours in Canada Court and Clifton Lodge are taking their landlord, the housing association PA Housing, to court over homes they say are unfit to live in. Keisha says her top-floor flat reaches 43C in a heatwave Even the landlord half-concedes the ground: its chief executive accepts that a growing number of residents face "uncomfortably warm temperatures … due to the changing climate", in homes "designed to keep heat in rather than keep them cool". Keisha is exactly the tenant the state's new cooling grant might have been written for. But as a social tenant, she is barred from it. Baroness Brown's committee finds the most deprived neighbourhoods are more than seven times as likely to be badly exposed to heat. The government had a long-running scheme for supporting upgrades to social housing - ECO - but it will close after this year over reports of "cowboy" installations. The replacement scheme, if it continues under the new government, will not start until next year. There is a cruel physics beneath the financial unfairness. Air conditioning doesn't destroy heat, it moves it - out of the flat and into the street, where, Santamouris says, it warms the air your neighbours breathe and drives up the demand for still more cooling, by about a third in his studies of Sydney. The machines keeping the financially comfortable cool make everyone else's nights worse; and as wealthier households cool their rooms, the rest fall further behind. A thermal divide, opening street by street. And it lands on the electricity grid at the worst possible moment. The electricity demand for cooling peaks on still, hot evenings - just as the wind drops and solar fades, leaving gas to supply the extra energy. In so doing, further greenhouse gas emissions are generated, adding bit by bit to the climate change effect – the very one driving the temperatures and the demand for air conditioning. And the same heat that drives the demand also weakens the supply: gas turbines lose output as the air warms, and in June several UK plants had to be turned down. But such is the scale of the heat that people are voting with their wallets - demand for portable air con units is through the roof, regardless of grants and the environment. The evidence from experts is that we should not go down this road. Santamouris and Baroness Brown reach for the same answer: passive cooling first, machines where genuinely needed, clean power behind them, and the lesson that France learned painfully in the deadly heatwave of 2003 - the vulnerable protected rather than left to improvise. Cooling every home by machine would strain the grid and warm the streets, hampering the effort to slow the warming that drives the demand. In Tokyo, Santamouris says, so many air conditioners now pump their waste heat into the air that the exhaust alone generates heat that's measured at close to a thousand watts of warming on every square metre - as much energy as falls from the sky at midday. "It's another sun," he adds with emphasis, "another sun." "It's not the same in London. But if we continue in the same way, in some years we will have the same results." The heat of this year and last, and the prospects of it being repeated, is a future Jo Shields is upset by. "It's our survival," she says. Most days, she tries to bury the thought of it - "because otherwise it terrifies me." Meanwhile, Mandy says she is grateful that the new community room with its air conditioning is providing some immediate respite for her and her mum. "We sit there all day with it on, it helps so much I want one in my flat."
