title: The life-altering choices immigrant families are making under Trump’s crackdown | CNN
description: A quiet upheaval is unfolding in homes, schools, churches and workplaces across the United States, as families try to prepare for – or avoid – an encounter with immigration authorities.
content: A quiet upheaval is unfolding in homes, schools, churches and workplaces across the United States, as families try to prepare for –– or avoid –– an encounter with immigration authorities. Some have left the United States after decades of building lives here. Others have considered giving up their unborn child for adoption, so the baby could have a better future. Parents are naming guardians for their children in case they are detained or deported, while others have stopped working, shopping or even leaving home, relying instead on neighbors and churches. The choices are deeply personal. Some are irreversible. Emma Confesor was pregnant with her fourth child when a question she had never imagined began keeping her awake: Would her baby have a better future raised by someone else? Confesor, 39, emigrated from Puebla, Mexico, more than two decades ago. But uncertainty surrounding President Donald Trump’s effort to end birthright citizenship led her to consider placing her unborn child up for adoption. “It didn’t seem fair to me that the baby wouldn’t have citizenship,” Confesor said through tears. “I had considered adoption so the baby could have a better future.” For weeks, the possibility consumed her. She said she struggled to sleep, afraid her child could be denied the future she believed every baby born in the United States should have. Confesor was not alone. Civil rights groups ask judge to block Trump’s new birthright citizenship order In an ACLU lawsuit challenging Trump’s executive order, another pregnant woman said she became so desperate to ensure her son would be born a US citizen that she asked her doctor whether labor could be induced early so he would arrive before the policy could take effect. Her doctor advised against it. Then came the decision that changed everything. On June 30, the Supreme Court ruled that the 14th Amendment guarantees birthright citizenship, rejecting the administration’s effort to end automatic citizenship for children born on U.S. soil to many noncitizen parents. For Confesor, the fear that had dominated her pregnancy began to lift. “I feel relieved,” she said. “I kept thinking, ‘It’s not fair.’ I wasn’t sleeping well because I was worried this could affect me. Not just me, but so many mothers who are going to have babies here.” While Confesor feared for her baby’s future, other parents were preparing for the possibility that they would not be there to raise their children who were born US citizens. In Maryland, a Salvadoran mother signed legal papers naming Father Vidal Rivas, the priest at her local church, as temporary guardian of her 7-year-old son if she and her husband were deported. “It’s not easy to sign a document where it feels like you’re handing your child over to someone else,” she told CNN affiliate Univision through tears. The uncertainty, she said, had taken a toll. “I keep thinking and thinking… I feel like my health has suffered because you just don’t know,” she said. “Honestly, I’ve stayed in my house, just praying that God’s will be done.” She is part of a growing number of immigrant parents making contingency plans in case they are detained or deported. Many families have already been forced into separation. A CNN investigation published last September found more than 100 US citizen children , from newborns to teenagers, had been left without their parents after immigration enforcement actions. Some were taken in by relatives, neighbors or family friends. Others entered foster care. At St. Matthew’s Episcopal Church in Hyattsville, Maryland, Rivas has been appointed standby legal guardian for at least 31 children whose parents fear they could be detained or deported “Many of these parents have no other relatives in the country,” Rivas said. “Some want their children to stay here. I would become legally responsible for them so they can continue going to school and have what they need. Other parents hope their children can finish high school before they are sent to reunite with them.” Rivas said he will serve as a guardian for as long as families need him. “It’s truly as if they were your own children,” he said. For others, departure has become the only choice that still feels like their own. Abdiel and Adilene Domínguez had built nearly their entire lives in Minnesota. Abdiel arrived from Mexico at six, Adilene as an infant, and both were protected under Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals , or DACA, which grants certain immigrants brought to the US as children temporary protection from deportation and authorization to work, but no permanent legal status. They married, raised four children, bought a home and opened a church in Minneapolis. New Trump rule makes it harder for some immigrants to get green cards But as immigration enforcement increased, they told CNN they became afraid to go to stores or send their children to school. Abdiel also said he was told his commercial driver’s license would be canceled. Instead of waiting to see what might happen, they sold their home, vehicles and belongings and left for Mexico. Seven months later, they were living with Abdiel’s mother in Morelos, where the children were struggling with Spanish and enrolling in school, and their parents were trying to adjust to a country that no longer felt familiar. “I don’t know anything about Mexico,” Adilene told CNN. “Everything I know is Minnesota. I’m in shock.” The Dominguezes left on their own, without using a federal program. But the pressure they described mirrors a broader Trump administration strategy encouraging immigrants to depart voluntarily . Project Homecoming, a $915 million initiative, offers free flights and stipends of up to $2,600 to immigrants who leave through the CBP Home app. An internal DHS document reviewed by CNN in March showed nearly 72,000 people had departed through the program; more than half were already in ICE detention when they enrolled. More than 72,000 immigration court cases also ended in voluntary departure so far in this fiscal year, compared with more than 35,000 the previous year. The consequences are also reshaping the lives of US citizens in mixed-status families. In Pittsburgh, CNN followed Julio Mendoza, an undocumented Mexican immigrant who had lived in the United States since he was 11, as he prepared to leave with his American wife, Sasha, and their three US-born children. Sasha said they feared Julio could be detained one day and simply not come home. Rather than risk that outcome, the entire family chose to move to Mexico together. “Everything we do, we do together,” Julio told CNN. For families who stay, the disruption often unfolds quietly, in the routines they begin to abandon. Across the country, immigrants have stayed home from work, kept children out of school and avoided stores, churches and other places that once anchored daily life. Jacobita Cortes, a United Methodist pastor in Chicago, said that fear has changed the rhythms of her community. “They’re afraid to go to the store, to the supermarket,” Cortes told CNN. “Where do our people go? To the supermarkets where you buy your tortillas, your meat; to the church where you go to thank God.” Some churches, she said, have moved services online, while congregations are helping families who are too afraid to leave home order groceries or arrange school pickups through neighbors and volunteers. “If someone needs somebody to go do their shopping, they only have to pick up the phone and call,” Cortes said. For parents who are afraid, she added, “find someone who can help, a neighbor or someone who can pick up the children from school.” The same pattern has surfaced elsewhere. In Minneapolis and New Orleans, CNN found once-bustling shops and restaurants growing quiet during federal immigration operations as some immigrants avoided work and parents kept children home from school. In Brooklyn’s Little Haiti, normally busy streets and businesses have grown quiet after the Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status for Haitians . Community leaders also warned of ripple effects in hospitals, nursing homes and home health care, where many Haitian immigrants work. For some immigrants, the fear is no longer confined to the possibility of deportation. It is reshaping what it means to live a life in the United States. title: Bulldozers rip into Big Bend National Park, driving anger and heartbreak | CNN
description: Environmentalists and a bipartisan coalition of state officials and border sheriffs are part of a growing chorus of opposition to ongoing border security amid the wilds of Big Bend National Park in Texas.
content: The towering cliffs, jagged mountain tops, and punishing desert climate of the Big Bend region in Texas have long proved to be the best barrier the United States could have with Mexico. For generations, the idea of needing to build physical structures to stop illegal migration was considered “insane,” as one former superintendent of Big Bend National Park said. But now the expansive reach of President Donald Trump’s southern border plan has stretched into this remote region that sees only about 1% of unauthorized crossing apprehensions. Bulldozers are clearing land in the beloved national park, where wildlife roams and the scenery has been untouched for thousands of years . “We didn’t have to worry about any type of barrier. We had a God-made barrier,” said Sheriff Thaddeus Cleveland of Terrell County, a vast and sparsely populated area northeast of the park. He spent 26 years in the US Border Patrol, hearing little if any talk of needing extra infrastructure in the area where he grew up, he said. “But that’s definitely changed.” US Customs and Border Protection says it’s not planning to build the same kind of 30-foot-high barrier that has appeared across parts of Arizona, California, New Mexico and Texas inside the national park. But critics say the plan that is in the works is no less destructive. Earlier this month, bulldozers were videoed uprooting trees and shoveling dirt as wild animals trotted by. They were doing preliminary work ahead of the budgeted $1.72 billion main construction project designated for the area inside Big Bend National Park, the agency said. It’s part of the bigger plan to finish the border wall — or some form of it — before Trump leaves office, with steel walls and vehicle barriers and hundreds of miles of new roads cutting through wildly remote areas. Those with concerns or outright opposition to the work in this remote desert wilderness run the gamut from a few elected Republicans to young activists, sweeping in a pro-border control sheriff and a retired National Park Service superintendent. Photographer Natalie Newman made a commitment to Big Bend back in February when then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem waived certain federal laws related to environmental safety, historic preservation and wildlife protection, among other initiatives, saying there was “an acute and immediate need to construct additional physical barriers and roads” in the Big Bend region. “It started out as just documenting the beauty of it, trying to get people to see why it’s special and what makes it special and what makes it so beautiful and worth protecting. But that has transformed just over the last week,” she told CNN, standing near Santa Elena Canyon, where tall cliffs rise nearly 1,500 feet high from the Rio Grande and where she first saw bulldozers working in the national park. “More than anything else, I feel heartbreak over all of this,” she said. Newman enjoys the wilder parts of this park that’s larger than the state of Rhode Island, where you may see fewer people than javelinas — a mammal that looks like a small wild pig, though it’s an entirely different species. Cacti and wildflowers bloom across the state and federal land around Big Bend, which coupled with even larger nature preserves across the border are part of the Chihuahuan desert, the largest such ecosystem in North America. But these days when her binoculars are trained on something in the distance, she’s more likely to be checking on the progress of road clearing than on any of the hundreds of bird species that frequent the park. She said she will keep sharing that news, doing her part to stand up for the national park. “I’m hopeful every single day that it’ll be the day that someone somewhere does something that puts a stop to it,” she said. If there is no stopping, retired park superintendent Bob Krumenaker said what could happen in Big Bend would rival the flooding of Hetch Hetchy Valley a century ago, an event that changed arguments about preserving the environment. It’s why he labels the whole plan “insane.” “If they continue with this and build most of the things they have talked about, or even a good fraction of those, this will be the biggest desecration of the national park system — not just Big Bend National Park — since they built a dam in a pristine valley in Yosemite National Park more than 100 years ago. This is a story that our children and grandchildren will be telling,” he told CNN. Compounding the natural destruction is the damage being done to people’s trust, Krumenaker added. “It’s just a tremendous erosion, if not violation, of the agreement that Texans and the American people made when they established that national park. The federal government that I worked for for 41 years is disrespecting its citizens in a in a huge way.” Krumenaker, now chairman of the Keep Big Bend Wild advocacy group, spent five years as superintendent of Big Bend National Park and is familiar not only with the multiple studies and approvals needed for any material changes, but also with his federal partners in Border Patrol and the need for security. “I totally support a secure border in Big Bend, but this is the least active place in the country for illegal border crossings,” he said. “This is purely political, and it will, it risks destroying one of the nation’s greatest places. It’s just horrible.” He recalled as superintendent having an annual budget of between $8 million and $9 million and a maintenance to-do list of about $100 million they would chip away at when they could. Those numbers are dwarfed by the $1.72 billion earmarked for the Big Bend work, part of the larger $46.5 billion allocated for border wall construction in Trump’s signature legislation, the “Big Beautiful Bill.” Sheriff Cleveland thought the talk of security construction was “BS” when he first heard of it. His experience in local and national law enforcement tells him a different story than that framed by CBP that Big Bend is “an area of high illegal entry.” What he calls the “God-given barriers” of steep mountains and valleys around the river and an undeveloped landscape without roads would prevent any vehicle getting to his patch. Yet new vehicle barriers are being planned for Terrell County, part of the total $7 billion scheme for the Big Bend sector of the border that includes the national park and land either side. In a statement to CNN, CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott said the agency is carrying out “survey and design work,” rather than the construction of a wall through the park. It involves building “one new access road, improving existing roads, installing detection technology, and placing vehicle barriers in limited, strategic locations,” he said. “We are working to preserve the landscape and protect the access visitors and local businesses depend on,” he added. “I believe in border security … but let’s put a barrier where a barrier makes sense,” Cleveland told CNN. “Let’s spend money where we need to spend the money.” Cleveland thinks using technology would be better support for him and other rural areas. He points to a solar-powered radar tower with a relatively small footprint that can scan the landscape and identify humans by their gait, triggering cameras to lock on and feed information to agents. Another option would be drones tracking people and helping responders plan a safe interception amid the rugged terrain, he said. “The biggest problem is the people making the decisions out here for the Big Bend sector have never stepped foot out here.” Cleveland ran for sheriff as a Republican but says he may switch to independent — what he sees as the profligate federal spending on something unnecessary does not mesh with his own fiscal conservatism. He signed a letter being carried around the area by former land commissioner Jerry Patterson, praising Trump for closing the border and asking the administration to consider cheaper and less destructive options for the Big Bend region. A similar approach is being taken by others in Texas. US Sen. John Cornyn wrote to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin last week urging him to meet with local stakeholders before any more construction proceeds on state or federal property. Some of Mullin’s involvement so far has been to waive another federal law, effectively ending a lawsuit claiming that law was being violated. Land Commissioner Dawn Buckingham was more forthright, sending a cease-and-desist letter warning of possible legal action to Customs and Border Protection after she said a federal contractor was sent to work in the Big Bend Ranch State Park without permission. The accompanying news release was titled “Don’t Tread on Texas.” On Friday, The People of La Junta for Preservation, an Indigenous-led preservation nonprofit, an outdoor recreation company and members of the Lipan Apache community asked a federal court to block the border wall construction on grounds the project threatens constitutionally protected religious freedoms. The suit, filed in San Antonio, states: “Once an archaeological site excavated by heavy machinery, once the physical context of artifacts is destroyed, or once a sacred or culturally significant landscape is permanently altered, the injury is irreparable.” The threatened areas, the suit contends, include places members of the Lipan Apache community use “for religious observance, ceremony, prayer, gathering, or other traditional religious practices.” CNN has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment. The nonprofit said they chose to pursue legal action because their “ancestors entrusted” them with the land. “For us, this is not an abstract policy debate,” the group said in a Facebook post Friday. “Our families have lived, prayed, gathered medicine, buried and reburied our ancestors, carried water, made offerings, and held ceremony along this river for generations beyond written memory. The river is not simply a boundary or a resource. She is living. She is a relative.” In a separate case filed in the nation’s capital, a federal judge on Friday rejected the Tohono O’odham Nation’s request to block border wall construction along parts of the Native American tribe’s reservation in Arizona. The Nation claimed the wall would trespass on its lands and diminish its boundaries without congressional authorization. US District Judge Richard Leon wrote “the Government’s interests in securing the border, enforcing immigration laws, and ensuring public safety outweigh any surviving irreparable harms at this juncture.” In a statement, Tohono O’odham Nation Chairman Verlon M. Jose disagreed and said the tribe “will consider all possible options for moving forward,” The Associated Press reported. Gov. Greg Abbott remarked before Trump entered the White House for the first time that he did not want a border wall across the entirety of his state. “There are serpentine regions of the Rio Grande where it would be extremely challenging to build a wall. There are parts like the Big Bend region — we don’t want (to) see a wall in the beautiful Big Bend National Park,” Abbott said in December 2016, as reported by The Associated Press . CNN asked for his current views and was directed to a previous statement from Abbott’s press secretary Andrew Mahaleris: “Rugged, isolated areas like Big Bend are great opportunities to deploy technology to aid in securing the border.” Critics say most statewide elected Republican officials have been too quiet in their condemnation of the border barrier construction projects because they fear the wrath of Trump’s criticism on his signature issue of border security. “The one person who is supposed to stand for Texas right now, our governor, is silent,” resident Jess Bartko said. “What they are doing is actively waging a war against our parks, our public lands, our community and our livelihoods.” On Wednesday, Bartko and about 100 other protesters gathered by the river, whose route gives the area its name and which attracts many of the half-million or so annual visitors to the national park. Tourism is a big deal here — for running the river and watching the night sky. There are worries that both will be impacted. As far as the upheaval, there could be debris in the river, and construction lights from sites and worker camps could pollute some of the darkest sky in the Lower 48, blurring the star-filled views of the cosmos. This week some roads and facilities were closed in the national park because of the construction. Down at the river, beside the entrance to Santa Elena Canyon, one of the “crown jewels” of the park, the demonstrators whooped and hollered, their shouts echoing off the cliff walls as they pledged to keep working to protect Big Bend. “The land remembers, the water remembers, it will remember us and our fight,” Joan Escamilla told her fellow supporters of the national park. “You can bury my heart in the Rio Grande.” This story has been updated with additional information. © 2026 Cable News Network. title: Teen charged with murder of mother and brother used ChatGPT to create ‘fantasy stories’ about killing family, officials say | CNN
description: A Massachusetts teen charged in the double murder of his mother and younger brother had used the artificial intelligence chatbot ChatGPT to search for “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories” about the killing of his family, prosecutors have said.
content: A Massachusetts teen charged in the double murder of his mother and younger brother had used the artificial intelligence chatbot ChatGPT to search for “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories” about the killing of his family, prosecutors have said. A plea of not guilty was entered Thursday for Arjun Aravind, 17, on two counts of murder, two counts of assault and battery on a family or household member and other charges. His mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his brother, Siddharth Aravind, 14, were found dead Tuesday in their home in Acton, some 20 miles northwest of Boston, prosecutors said . Arjun Aravind “had recently been demonstrating some concerning behavior, including using the internet and ChatGPT to make searches for theoretical ideas or fantasy stories regarding the killing of his family,” Middlesex County District Attorney Marian Ryan told reporters Wednesday, citing the law enforcement investigation. “He was engaged in the use of ChatGPT in creating fantasy stories, kind of the Gothic novel kind of stories, asking questions, creating characters, asking what about this, if this happened to that, and they seem to appear to relate to threats to his family not surviving,” Ryan said . A “heavily damaged bloody laptop,” and “a bent utensil, possible [sic] a knife with an orange handle” were found at the scene, a police report obtained by CNN affiliate WCVB indicated. Venkatesan’s and Siddharth’s causes of death are still pending, Ryan said. Aravind over the past year had had behavior issues and his family had hidden knives from him, the teen’s father said, WCVB reported, citing police reports. The teen did not realize his mother and brother were dead until after he was arrested, his defense attorney, Debra DeWitt, told WCVB. CNN has asked her for comment. AI technology allegedly has been linked to other criminal acts, and Florida this spring sued ChatGPT owner OpenAI , alleging the tool had “no parental oversight,” got minors addicted, caused users to lose “critical thinking skills,” helped mass shooters and encouraged suicide. OpenAI believes minors “need significant protection” and has “put in place industry leading protections and policies,” it has said. CNN reached out Friday to OpenAI about this week’s murder case. Aravind was ordered held without bail and to undergo a mental health evaluation. A probable cause hearing was set for September 11. Florida sues OpenAI, alleging it’s unsafe for children Police responded Tuesday to his family home after a tutor arrived for a scheduled visit and could not get in, Ryan said Wednesday in a news conference. The teen’s father was then notified and requested a wellness check. Officers found the two victims inside – but not Aravind, who was believed to have fled using his mother’s 2014 green Honda Accord, she said. While responding to a separate incident Wednesday morning, police in neighboring Wayland found Aravind in his mother’s car in a parking lot and took him into custody. The family had only recently moved to Acton for “better schools and support system for the kids,” DeWitt said. “We put an enormous weight on our kids … We know the kids will be seeing and reading about this, likely on social media,” Ryan said. “This is an unspeakable tragedy. It is an incredibly dark day – obviously, an insurmountable tragedy for the dad in this case.” © 2026 Cable News Network. A Warner Bros. Discovery Company. All Rights Reserved. title: Jalen Brunson on the ever-growing love story between the game of golf and basketball | CNN
description: There is an ever-growing love story between the game of golf and basketball. CNN Sports talked with New York Knicks star Jalen Brunson about the connection.
content: There is an ever-growing love story between the game of golf and basketball . Maybe it’s the rhythm of a smooth swing mirroring the comfort of a polished jumper. Maybe it’s the chance to perform outside in front of chirping birds rather than chirping fans inside a booming arena. For NBA champion and Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, it’s simpler than that – it’s competition. “My dad stopped playing me one-on-one on the court, so I needed to find something else to beat him in,” Brunson told CNN Sports . “You’re still being competitive.” Brunson’s dad, Rick Brunson, was also an NBA player and is currently an assistant coach for the New York Knicks . “There are a lot of players around the league who bring clubs on the road when you’re going to warm cities,” the younger Brunson said. “It’s become a thing.” The offseason especially has turned into showcase opportunities for players across social media and beyond, either casually or in tournament form. Brunson’s annual charity golf classic fits right in. It raises money for his Second Round Foundation, which pulls on his story as a second-round draft pick to provide opportunities to “the overlooked” and stresses “success doesn’t always look like a first-round pick,” the foundation’s mission statement reads. “You can go down so many different roads with that term,” Brunson told CNN. “I felt like I was overlooked in sport, but there are a lot of kids and people who overlooked this in life.” He co-founded the foundation with his mom, Sandra Brunson. “Overlooked is a term that I think many people can associate with,” but for children “everyone needs to start on the same playing field and we’re just happy to be able to help and to provide whatever resources we can,” Sandra Brunson told CNN Sports. For the golf fundraiser, Brunson said he typically sends invites out to other players, like teammate Josh Hart, but that people also sign up on their own before his mom cut him off. “I send the invites, OK? So if anybody didn’t get one, it’s on me,” Sandra said. Jalen laughed and said, “I mean, I was gonna throw her under the bus anyway.” LeBron James , whom Brunson is scheduled to be facing on opening day of the coming NBA season, is among the basketball elite attempting to climb the golfing ladder. Others, more notoriously prolific on the course, like Steph Curry, Los Angeles Lakers star Austin Reaves, Michael Jordan, and even recently retired guard JR Smith have arguably climbed that ladder. Curry won the 2023 American Century Classic, a premier celebrity tournament that includes many pro athletes. Reaves has a fully dedicated golf social media Instagram account , and right after retirement from the NBA, Smith joined the golf team at North Carolina A&T as a freshman walk-on. Even Caitlin Clark and Diana Taurasi on the WNBA side have not been shy about their golf bug. The NBA posted a video of Philadelphia 76ers star Tyrese Maxey on the course as he jokingly admitted, “I can do all this basketball with 20,000 people but golfing in front of cameras? Can’t do it.” The PGA published an article citing specific basketball movements that “closely relate to the golf swing and golf performance,” including: free throws compared with putting, the crossover compared with the tempo change during a swing, and more. For Brunson, though, it’s not that deep – yet. “It can be,” he said. “But I’m getting there.” “There’s a lot surrounding it that makes it like the perfect getaway for a lot of not just basketball players but pro athletes,” Brunson said, correctly mentioning the golf phenomenon is nowhere near limited solely to basketball. But on how prevalent it is in the NBA, he says, “It’s definitely a good group … It’s a perfect getaway where you’re still being competitive.” One person in the Brunson orbit who hasn’t quite been able to break into the game of golf is Jalen’s mom. “No one in my family has ever even attempted to invite me to a golf outing to participate,” Sandra told CNN Sports. “I haven’t seen her even touch a club,” Jalen joked. “And we’re trying to play, we’re not – this isn’t a lesson.” “My daughter has clubs. My granddaughter has clubs, I don’t even have clubs,” Sandra said. But it’s also the focal point of their annual charity event so she anticipates her competitiveness as a former collegiate athlete will get her there at some point. This offseason for Jalen has meant less golf as he recovers from a wrist surgery, but it’s also meant more downtime, valuable moments with family, and even an upcoming children’s book . Still, the first offseason as an NBA champion has been a little “hectic,” he explained, but in the end “all great problems to have.” In about two short months, the NBA regular season will officially kick off, but if the volume of offseason golf is any indication, the competitiveness started well before that opening tip. © 2026 Cable News Network. description: In our roundup of travel stories this week: why mosquitoes are getting better at outsmarting humans, the sun-kissed island known as the “Turkish Maldives,” plus the mysterious case of the missing Korean trash cans.
content: Sign up for Unlocking the World, CNN Travel’s weekly newsletter . Get news about destinations, plus the latest in aviation, food and drink, and where to stay. In our roundup of travel stories this week: why mosquitoes are getting better at outsmarting humans, the sun-kissed island known as the “Turkish Maldives,” plus the mysterious case of the missing Korean trash cans. Tacos or tarte tatin? Burritos or boeuf Bourguignon? Choose your fighter as we’re going all in on a battle of national fare. France has the haute cuisine, the Michelin pedigree and the UNESCO-recognized bread. Mexico has the confluence of Indigenous and European influences, the slow-cooked meat, and the pre-Hispanic corn processes. We’ve put together a roundup of 20 classic French dishes everyone needs to try and, because we were feeling generous, 23 Mexican dishes that ought to be on your table ASAP. Following up with the cheese course, we have cancoillotte , a 2,000-year-old low-fat, high-protein cheese currently taking over French dairy aisles. For US-based subscribers, we also have a two-tier dessert: The full CNN Original series of Eva Longoria: Searching for Mexico and Eva Longoria: Searching for France are available to stream right now. Stay safe out there this summer. Video captured recently in Botswana shows the terrifying moment a tourist boat had to outpace a charging hippo. Take a look : Its butterfly stroke is Olympic level. On the smaller end of the scale, scientists are discovering mosquitoes are smarter than we thought. The blood-besotted blighters are the world’s deadliest animal , and they’ve developed plenty of tricks to tap our veins, including remembering people who’ve tried to swat them. And now we go tinier again, with a warning about microscopic pathogens. Louisiana health officials are urging Gulf Coast beachgoers to take precautions amid a surge in infections caused by a flesh-eating bacteria found in coastal waters. Vibrio vulnificus thrive in heat and this past July was the hottest month in the US since records began. Continuing our countdown of America’s Best Towns to Visit in 2026 , we have Bethlehem, Pennsylvania , at No. 4. August is here, the days are getting shorter — shouldn’t you be thinking of getting the Christmas tree down from the attic? Or better yet, take a trip to Bethlehem, a former American steel town with serious holiday spirit. “The festivities begin early here,” the manager of one of two Christmas-themed stores open year-round on Main Street tells CNN. “It’s like living in a snow globe or a Hallmark movie.” Bethlehem’s rich legacy as a historic 18th-century Moravian settlement has also earned recognition as one of the United States’ newest UNESCO World Heritage sites. Take a look, too, at the rest of our list so far: Roanoke, Virginia , at No. 10, Lawrence, Kansas , at No. 9, Iowa City, Iowa at No. 8, Juneau, Alaska , at No. 7, Burlington, Vermont , at No. 6 and Fort Collins, Colorado , at No. 5. It’s never too early to start planning your 2027 vacation. Less than an hour off the coast of the Turkish Riviera lies Suluada –- a remote island so strikingly white and blue it’s earned the nickname “the Turkish Maldives.” Accessible only by boat and completely untouched, CNN’s Leroy Ah Ben explores this gem known mostly to locals. Uganda’s Ssese Islands are one of the few places in the world where a tropical archipelago sits inside a landlocked country. In the middle of Lake Victoria, Africa’s largest lake, the islands are a magical landscape where locals and pilgrims connect with ancient spirits at a sacred waterfall. With just 7,000 public trash cans on the streets for a city of nearly 10 million people, Seoul residents and tourists can struggle to find one. CNN's Yoonjung Seo goes on a mission to find the nearest trash can. Seoul is a city of nearly 10 million people, but there are just 7,000 public trash cans on its streets. CNN’s Yoonjung Seo went on a mission to find the nearest receptacle. Tourists visiting Japan also struggle to find trash cans but the reasons behind that are very different. A stellar spectacle. A White House shakeup. A massive jackpot. What do you remember from the week that was ? Meet the corgis leading hiking groups. Their legs may be short, but their strength is mighty. Watch here . title: Jason Arday: Former Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism found dead | CNN
description: Jason Arday, a former University of Cambridge professor, was found dead in London on Friday, just days after resigning over questions surrounding his career.
content: Jason Arday, a former University of Cambridge professor, was found dead in London on Friday, just days after resigning over questions surrounding his career. A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police told CNN that a 41-year-old man was found unresponsive in Battersea, south London, and was later pronounced dead at the scene. The spokesperson said the death was “treated as as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.” While the force did not name Arday, British media widely reported that he was the man found dead in Battersea. Arday, a sociologist, was celebrated as the youngest ever Black professor at Cambridge until last month, when allegations of plagiarism in his academic work and questions surrounding claims about his athletic and fundraising accomplishments began to swirl in the media. The university’s Vice-Chancellor Deborah Prentice said in a statement on Friday that the university was “desperately saddened to hear this tragic news.” “Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time,” she added in the statement posted on X. When Arday resigned in early August, he defended himself, saying his decision to step down “should not be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship.” “Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me,” he said. “It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure.” News of his death on Friday caused shock waves online, with many criticizing some of the coverage that led to and followed his resignation. “Quite a bit of the British media should ask themselves some serious questions as to whether the tenor and volume of the coverage they gave to this man was remotely proportionate,” journalist Lewis Goodall said on X. The Good Law Project, a campaign group that has supported Arday since the allegations first emerged, said Arday’s death was “a tragedy for him and those who loved him.” The group’s executive director Jo Maugham said in a statement that people around Arday “had been warning the media that this was a risk.” “I do not understand what the public interest was in continuing to hound him after he resigned as a professor and I do not understand what risk assessments media outlets did,” he added. Lucy Powell, the UK’s secretary of state for education, said she was “shocked and saddened” to hear about Arday’s death. “My heartfelt condolences are with his friends and family at this very sad time. I urge people to give them privacy through this incredibly difficult period (and) to remember there are real people with loved ones involved.” Cambridge initially stood by Arday when questions about his qualifications were raised publicly by the British press and a one-time philosophy researcher who left the university after his critique of diversity, equity and inclusion programs. The university said at the time that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday’s doctorate. It later opened an investigation, “following new information about Professor Arday’s qualifications and honorary appointments,” it said in a statement. Earlier this week, the university said that Durham and Glasgow Universities were also investigating the circumstances surrounding Arday’s academic posts there. title: Luigi Mangione: What’s next after federal guilty plea in killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO | CNN
description: Luigi Mangione’s guilty plea to federal charges in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson raises questions about the future of his state murder trial.
content: More than a year after the fatal shooting of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, 28-year-old Luigi Mangione confessed to the killing in his own words as he pleaded guilty to federal charges in court Friday – a move that raises questions about the future of his upcoming state murder trial. “On the morning of December 4, 2024, I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” Mangione said as he sat in a federal courtroom flanked by his defense attorneys. He spoke calmly – and expressed no remorse for murdering the 50-year-old healthcare executive and father of two as Thompson’s family members, including his widow, sat in the front row of the courtroom and held one another. The change of plea is a stunning development in a case that has captured national attention and exposed deep-seated frustration with the American healthcare system, as Mangione amassed a horde of devoted followers who sympathized with his cause and held him up as a kind of folk hero . Mangione faced both state and federal charges: His guilty plea staves off his federal trial on two stalking charges, which had been scheduled for January 2027. But the fate of Mangione’s state case , set to go to trial next month, now hangs in the balance as his attorneys seek to get second-degree murder and weapons charges dismissed over double jeopardy protections. A legal showdown that will likely delay the state trial is sure to follow, as the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office signaled Friday it would fight to see its prosecution proceed. Luigi Mangione’s defense team filed motions to dismiss state charges against him, arguing double jeopardy applies after Mangione pleaded guilty to federal stalking charges in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. CNN’s Kara Scannell reports state prosecutors intend to fight and litigate against the motion. Whether it does remains to be seen, but legal experts said Mangione’s defense has a strong argument that could see most of the state charges dismissed under New York state’s double jeopardy law, which goes further than the US Constitution in prohibiting two prosecutions based on the same criminal act or conduct. “I think it’s more likely than not that the state case goes away with the federal guilty plea,” said Anthony Capozzolo, a former prosecutor with the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office and a former federal prosecutor with the Eastern District of New York. Capozzolo expects New York prosecutors will be blocked from moving ahead “because it’s likely both offenses will be punishing someone for the murder of the same victim and the elements of the federal and state cases are punishing the same harm or evil.” “Therefore, the offenses will not be deemed different enough to allow New York to continue to prosecute the case,” he said. Mangione’s guilty plea in the federal case came during a conference which was hastily scheduled hours after he appeared in state court earlier this week to discuss the upcoming trial. CNN reported this week Mangione’s defense attorneys were in plea negotiations with federal prosecutors – although his defense attorneys confirmed in court Friday no agreement was reached. US Judge Margaret Garnett set Mangione’s sentencing for December 18 . He faces a maximum sentence of life in prison; if the DA’s office is satisfied with his federal sentence, it could agree to dismiss the state charges. For the first time Friday, Mangione publicly described Thompson’s killing in his own words, detailing the steps he took to plan the shooting outside a Midtown Manhattan hotel hosting UnitedHealthcare’s annual investor conference. Mangione spoke quickly, prompting the judge to interrupt him because she was having trouble hearing. “After years of enduring severe pain from a broken back, navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system and witnessing similar experiences of countless others, I learned that UnitedHealthcare would be holding its annual investor conference in New York City on December 4, 2024,” Mangione said, adding the conference would be attended by investors and executives but not medical providers or patients. Mangione used a 3D printer to create part of a firearm, he said, which he equipped with a silencer and magazine before travelling to New York City in November 2024. “I then emailed UnitedHealthcare leadership, posing as an investor at a firm managing over $50 billion in assets and requesting information about the conference,” Mangione said. “Unlike my previous interactions with insurers, I received an immediate response within an hour.” Reading a prepared statement with little emotion, Mangione described shooting Thompson: “When I did so, I understood that my actions would place him in fear of death or serious bodily injury. I knew what I was doing was illegal.” He did not look at Thompson’s family. Thompson’s killing outside a Midtown Manhattan hotel ignited a multistate manhunt that ended five days later, when police in Altoona, Pennsylvania, arrested Mangione in a McDonald’s. In his backpack, authorities said, they found a gun that linked him to the crime scene and a notebook that included writings about targeting the CEO at the “parasitic bean-counter convention” – strong evidence experts previously told CNN would narrow his defense options at trial . Mangione’s lawyers raised concerns when he was first charged in both jurisdictions that the 28-year-old was unfairly being tried twice for the same crime. Since then, the prospect of double jeopardy has remained an open question that’s come up several times during open court proceedings and in filings. Manhunt: Tracking the CEO Murder Suspect Immediately following the federal hearing Friday, Mangione’s defense team filed a motion asking New York Judge Gregory Carro to dismiss second-degree murder and weapons charges in his state case, Karen Friedman Agnifilo told reporters outside the federal courthouse Friday. “It was a single tragic event, yet he’s being prosecuted twice for the same conduct,” she told reporters. “Thankfully, New York law does not allow this,” Friedman Agnifilo said. “New York law does not permit a person to be prosecuted and punished twice for the exact same crime under a statute that governs successive prosecutions.” In its filing, the defense asked the state judge to dismiss the charges, accusing federal and state prosecutors of coordinating their cases “to maximize the punitive effectiveness of the two cases at the expense of Mr. Mangione.” Mangione’s defense claimed state and federal prosecutors cut a deal to allow the state case to proceed first in an effort to evade double jeopardy protections and give both offices an opportunity to prosecute Mangione, violating the killer’s constitutional rights. “This coordinated deal between them had a specific purpose: The scheme was designed solely to ensure dual successive prosecutions, in order to attempt to avoid double jeopardy protections,” the filing said. The Manhattan District Attorney’s Office acknowledged Mangione’s motion to dismiss the state charges Friday afternoon but said it was ready to fight for its case in court. “We are encouraged that Mr. Thompson’s family received a measure of accountability today. While federal sentencing is pending, we are prepared to litigate the defense motions. The Manhattan D.A.’s Office remains committed to seeking justice for Mr. Thompson and his family,” a spokesperson said. Carro now must consider whether to allow the trial to move forward on all eight charges Mangione presently faces in the indictment. He could delay the September 8 start of jury selection while the parties argue in court filings – or even wait for the federal sentencing to play out before deciding. Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty Friday to federal stalking charges, telling the court he posed as an investor to obtain information about UnitedHealthcare’s 2024 conference, which CEO Brian Thompson was scheduled to attend. “I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” Mangione said during his allocution to the court. “I knew what I was doing was illegal.” Either side could appeal Carro’s decision, which would likely further delay a possible state trial – if it proceeds at all. New York legal experts have suggested state prosecutors are unlikely to see a trial against Mangione now that he’s resolved the federal case. “I do believe that based upon the law that the state trial goes away. I do think that this double jeopardy argument is real,” CNN legal analyst and criminal defense attorney Joey Jackson said, because both cases involve “the same sort of transaction and occurrence, the same set of facts,” and the same “evil” that is “eradicated” by Mangione’s plea Friday. Stacy Schneider, a New York City criminal defense attorney, told CNN’s Jake Tapper Mangione’s defense has a “calculated, good shot” at getting the state case dismissed, “but not a slam dunk.” “They want to invoke the New York state double jeopardy law, which is a broad law, and says not only can you not prosecute them for the same act – but you can’t prosecute them for the same act or criminal transaction, even though it’s two different offenses,” she said. Prosecutors, meanwhile, will likely argue “the act of stalking was a prelude to the murder,” Schneider said, and that the acts encompassed by the federal charges are “not the same as actually pulling the trigger.” Whatever happens with the state case, experts said, Mangione will also likely be looking ahead to his sentencing in December, when he will have another opportunity to address the court. His attorneys will likely present what’s known as mitigating evidence, which the judge would weigh in determining his sentence. After Friday’s court appearance, Mangione’s defense attorney said Mangione has “accepted full responsibility” for Thompson’s death, calling Friday a “solemn and significant day.” “As Luigi explained in court today, he endured years of severe, debilitating pain following a broken back while struggling to navigate our healthcare and health insurance systems,” Friedman Agnifilo said outside the courthouse. “Like the thousands of people who have reached out since this tragedy to share their own experiences, he believed that the system had failed him and destroyed his life.” In a statement, Thompson’s family called the guilty plea “an important step toward justice,” and noted Mangione’s pending cases in New York and Pennsylvania state court. The latter case involves charges stemming from his arrest. “While nothing will ease the pain of losing him, we are grateful that the federal justice system has held the person responsible for this heinous act accountable,” the Thompson family said in their statement. “Now we look to the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of this crime.” CNN’s August Phillips contributed to this report. © 2026 Cable News Network. title: The obsession with ‘Mamdani marts’ isn’t about groceries | CNN Business
description: Whenever Mayor Zohran Mamdani offers new details about his plan to open five government-owned supermarkets in New York City, photos of Boris Yeltsin start circulating on social media.
content: Markets Hot Stocks Fear & Greed Index Latest Market News Hot Stocks Whenever Mayor Zohran Mamdani offers new details about his plan to open five government-owned supermarkets in New York City, photos of Boris Yeltsin start circulating on social media. Taken during Yeltsin’s trip to America months before the fall of the Soviet Union in 1989, the photos show the former Russian president astonished by the variety of frozen foods at Randall’s supermarket in Houston. Yeltsin tasted free cheese samples and surveyed the fish. He left the store with a goodie bag. On the flight after the impromptu stop, Yeltsin sat motionless with his head in his hands, considering the bare shelves of Soviet food markets. “What have they done to our poor people?” he said , according to his biography. Then, as now, America’s supermarkets are a marvel of the free market. The idea that government, which has been defined as incompetent and inefficient for decades, could provide grocery abundance and variety better than Walmart and Costco has triggered a visceral reaction among critics. They imagine “Mamdani marts” ending up like dreary state-run Soviet stores with one type of soup. The response to Mamdani’s plan reflects something much deeper than the brand of ketchup public stores will sell or the price of eggs. It comes down to a fundamental disagreement about the responsibility of government. Where supporters see government intervening to solve problems of everyday people struggling to afford groceries, others see a socialist mayor overreaching to take aim at a powerful symbol of America’s riches. “The debate is not really about the specific mechanics of the model,” said Nevin Cohen, an associate professor at the CUNY School of Public Health. It’s a “test of competing ideas about what we expect government to provide.” Never mind that the public stores aren’t a radical new idea and the city is bringing in private operators to manage them and source the food. Or that 99% of New Yorkers will never shop at one of them. They will not destroy John Castimatidis’ Gristedes supermarket empire . The American supermarket, with its endless array of products and innovations like the shopping cart and barcodes, has achieved an almost mythical status around the world. Supermarkets helped America project democracy abroad and win the Cold War. For decades, the U.S. Information Agency distributed images of supermarkets to promote the benefits of the “American way of life.” They are a bounty of consumer choice. Between 1960 and 2010, the number of different products in an average US supermarket grew from 6,000 to 47,000. New business models such as Walmart supercenters, Costco warehouse clubs and Trader Joe’s specialty stores expanded the abundance further. “Food is a potent symbol and catalyst for people’s politics,” said Tracey Deutsch, a historian at the University of Minnesota who studies food and capitalism. Stores were contested sites during the civil rights movement and the pandemic , she noted. “There’s a sense that grocery stores are the last bastion,” she said. “Grocery stores are places where people make their stand for the world they want.” Supporters of private sector solutions to address food insecurity say New York City should make it easier for Walmart to open or pay for Costco memberships for people who can’t afford them. But Mamdani’s animating political philosophy is to use government to solve everyday problems in people’s lives. He is following in the footsteps of his political idol, Mayor Fiorello LaGuardia, a champion of government intervention during the New Deal who built public parks, housing and the airport that bears his name. Overcoming opposition from private industry, LaGuardia opened a network of city-run indoor markets during the 1930s to move pushcart vendors off streets and reduce the cost of groceries. Several of the markets are open today. Mamdani wants to turn the vacant sites, still owned by the city, into public grocery stores. LaGuardia “believed in a simple definition of the task of government to make people’s lives better,” Mamdani said last month. “We are one step closer to fulfilling that fundamental responsibility.” Most stock quote data provided by BATS.
