title: Defending champion Gauff eliminated from French Open - Sport - DAWN.COM
description: A double fault in the next game brought Gauff two break-back points, but gutsy play allowed Potapova to hold.
content: Get the latest news and updates from Dawn PARIS: Reigning French Open champion Coco Gauff lost in three sets to Austrian Anastasia Potapova to end to her Roland Garros title defence on Saturday. The fourth seed was defeated in the third round 4-6, 7-6 (7/1), 6-4 by the 28th seed after being a break up in the deciding set. “I think I’ve had a few (big wins) before, but I’d put it top three for sure,” Potapova said on court after earning a career third win over Gauff. Despite losing her first service game to open the match, Gauff struck back to break the Russian-born Austrian in the eighth and 10th games and take the lead. Potapova responded with two consecutive breaks of her own to race 3-0 ahead at the start of the second frame. The 25-year-old’s serve then deserted her as well, as the next five games all produced breaks, with Potapova passing up two set points behind her own delivery. Gauff responded to that reprieve by earning her first hold of the set to force Potapova to serve again for the frame. The two-time major winnerbroke the world number 30 to level at 5-5 before holding again. But Potapova then refound her own serve to force a tie-break. A double fault dropped Gauff 5-0 behind, before she finally got on the board when Potapova overcooked a backhand. It was too little, too late, however, as the Austrian powered to the next two points and sent the match into a deciding set. Gauff drew first blood in the decider, pouncing on Potapova’s serve in the third game to nose in front, before being pegged back to 3-3. A double fault in the next game brought Gauff two break-back points, but gutsy play allowed Potapova to hold. A booming backhand winner down the line and a miss-hit Gauff forehand from deuce put Potapova 5-4 ahead with the world number four serving to keep her title defence alive. But from 30-0, Gauff quickly unravelled and Potapova fell on her back in celebration as the American returned long and departed the tournament. Potapova will meet Russian 22nd seed Anna Kalinskaya for a spot in the quarter-finals. Earlier on Saturday, Naomi Osaka continued to shine in the City of Light as she beat American teenager Iva Jovic 7-6(7/5), 6-7(3/7), 6-4 to set up a last-16 clash against world number one Aryna Sabalenka. Sabalenka eased past Daria Kasatkina 6-0, 7-5 to continue her pursuit of a first French Open title.The clash between Osaka and Sabalenka could tempt the event organisers, who have been criticised for only scheduling men in the marquee late slots, to put a woman’s match on at night. Meanwhile, The Belarusian top seed Sabalenka ripped through the first set in 29 minutes and faced resistance in the second but completed the win in one hour and 17 minutes, and become the ninth woman to win 100 matches while ranked No.1. Osaka won their only meeting at a major, at the same stage in the 2018 US Open. Since then they had not met again until two encounters this season — both won by Sabalenka at Indian Wells and Madrid. Meanwhile, Ukrainian Oleksandra Oliynykova, who in the build-up to her third-round match accused her Russian opponent Diana Shnaider of “taking money” from a “company financing war crimes” and of liking social media posts by “propagandists”, lost 7-5, 6-1. In the men’s section, Flavio Cobolli laid down a marker with an emphatic 6-2, 6-2, 6-3 victory over Learner Tien. Cobolli will next meet Zachary Svajda, who beat Francisco Cerundolo, with a spot in the quarters on the line. DJOKOVIC OUSTED In Friday’s late match, Brazilian teenager Joao Fonseca knocked Novak Djokovic out in the third round to scupper the Serbian great’s latest quest for a record 25th Grand Slam. Fonseca, 19, rallied from two sets down for the second straight match to stun the 39-year-old Djokovic with a phenomenal display of power-hitting. Fonseca triumphed 4-6, 4-6, 6-3, 7-5, 7-5 after four hours and 53 minutes to make the last 16 of a major for the first time. Djokovic’s exit comes a day after the shock elimination of world number one Jannik Sinner. It means there will be a first-time men’s Grand Slam champion this year at the French Open, ending a run of nine successive majors won by Sinner or Carlos Alcaraz. “What an incredible match to be part of,” said Djokovic, who had led by a break early in the final set but was unable to see it through. “Huge credit to Joao for really deserving to win the match. Without a doubt he was the better player in crucial moments.” Published in Dawn, May 31st, 2026 Compunode.com Pvt. Ltd. ( www.compunode.com ).Designed for Dawn . title: President calls for effective laws to curb tobacco use - Pakistan - DAWN.COM
description: Terms tobacco sellers "merchants of death".
content: Get the latest news and updates from Dawn • Terms tobacco sellers ‘merchants of death’ • Urges parents, teachers, health workers to raise awareness ISLAMABAD: President Asif Ali Zardari has underlined the need for effective legislation against tobacco use to protect people and future generations from the hazards of the “killer addiction”. “The time has come that, besides other issues, the national parliament and provincial legislatures should make laws and create effective enforcement mechanisms against tobacco use in order to protect our people and future generations and effectively resist the merchants of death,” the president said in his message on World No Tobacco Day, observed on May 31. He said that besides parliament and the government, pa­­­r­­ents, teachers, artists, poets, singers, musicians, actors, pla­y­­­­­­w­­­rights, healthcare professionals and community leaders all had a role in shaping awa­­­­reness, discouraging the use of tobacco products and creating an ecosystem to protect people. He said change at the household and community level cou­ld contribute meaningfully to national progress in public health. “As your elder and as your head of state, I must tell you that this day is a reminder of our shared responsibility to protect current and future generations from the harms of tobacco products,” President Zardari said. He said the World Health Organisation estimated that tobacco caused more than seven million deaths every year worldwide, including about 1.6 million deaths from second-hand smoke exposure. “These figures should compel us to reflect on the scale of a public health challenge that continues to affect millions of people and families,” he said. The president said children and young people remained particularly vulnerable as the tobacco and nicotine industry continued to target younger generations through evolving products and marketing approaches designed to create and sustain addiction. He said early exposure to nicotine heightened the risk of lifelong dependence and adverse health outcomes. President Zardari said the latest research showed that, globally and in Pakistan, the use of cigarettes, e-cigarettes, vaping devices, nicotine pouches and other nicotine products presented growing public health concerns. He said there was also evidence of concerning patterns of poly-substance use, where tobacco and nicotine products could coexist with other harmful substances, creating serious risks for young people and communities. He stressed that stronger awareness, regulation and prevention efforts were essential to check tobacco use. He said widespread second-hand smoke exposure increased children’s vulnerability to asthma, pneumonia, ear infections, low birth weight and sudden infant death. The impact extended beyond health, placing a heavy burden on families and health systems, he added. The president said tobacco products were also closely linked with a growing burden of non-communicable diseases, including cardiovascular disease, cancer and chronic respiratory conditions. Referring to the financial impact of tobacco-related illnesses, he said the issue was not abstract for many households. A working-age parent falling ill, repeated hospital visits, the cost of long-term treatment and reduced earning capacity could quickly strain already limited household resources, he said. title: Khaqan Shahnawaz wants you to check your privilege when bashing those Independence Day cake 'attack' videos - Celebrity - Images
description: He highlighted the abject poverty in which many Pakistanis live as well as the elite's role in keeping them there.
content: Actor and content creator Khaqan Shahnawaz wants you to check your privilege when commenting on those videos of people “attacking” cake on Independence Day. You know the ones — people scrambling and pushing each other in their rush to grab a slice or three, yelling and shouting and causing all sorts of uproar on social media where people label them “ignorant” and “the reason why Pakistan isn’t progressing”. Shahnawaz isn’t buying this criticism of uneducated people being the cause of their own ignorance. “They’re ignorant and uneducated because they were never taught anything. They weren’t given any opportunities. They didn’t grow up in Lahore, Karachi or Islamabad, or Sialkot, Gujranwala or Faisalabad. They are coming from villages,” he said in a video shared to his Instagram account on August 14. “Someone told you what happened on August 14, right? You weren’t born knowing what happened,” he addressed his followers. “Someone told you not to throw trash outside, even though you still do, I know. Someone told you not to attack cakes, because you get cake at home. You’ve tried cake before. If you were to see some Mano Salwa [divine food] somewhere and you didn’t know if you’d get any or if you’d ever get to have any in your life, you would attack it too,” he said. Poverty in Pakistan surged by seven per cent, pushing approximately 27 million additional people into financial distress over the last six years and bringing the total number of the impoverished population of the country to 70 million, according to this year’s Economic Survey. Pakistan measures poverty based on the cost of basic needs approach, in which the poverty line represents the minimum expenditure required to meet essential food and non-food needs. That means 70 million people definitely don’t have the means to buy and eat cake. “These things don’t happen all at once, it takes effort, and our governments, our leaders and we, the privileged class, have worked on it for the past 75 years to keep people like this,” Shahnawaz contended. “ “We also live in a bubble.” He referenced a video by a white content creator who made three videos with brands talking about how Pakistan is so great. “And it is great — for us. For the privileged class. It’s great for us, it’s great for foreigners. But go out and look at the main streets, people are out. That is the real Pakistan,” he said. “You’re saying Pakistan has been ruined because of them, no, it’s been ruined because of us. We have the education, we have the political power, we have the voice, we have the platform, we have the ability to debate, but we don’t do it. If someone comes and speaks against Pakistan we say, ‘no, no, show only positive side’, ‘why always talk negative’, or other nonsense like that,” he said. “Anyway, happy Independence to everyone. Before 1947, you didn’t have a political say, you couldn’t decide foreign policy, you paid tax that wasnt spent on you, education wasn’t that great, people used to say don’t educate your children, don’t give them a western education, the people wanting a western education for their kids would be abused, now things are very different, because we are free,” the actor said. “Before, we feared there was a majority religion that would dominate us, they would oppress us, now, there’s no such thing, no majority religion is oppressing another. So yeah, we are free, and for that, happy Independence Day, guys.” Compunode.com Pvt. Ltd. ( www.compunode.com ).Designed for Dawn .

title: Stars celebrate Independence Day with flags, families and prayers for Pakistan - Comment - Images
description: The mood was somewhat subdued this year after a number of crimes against women and children rocked the country.
content: Like every year, Pakistan’s celebrities fully embraced the country’s patriotic spirit on Independence Day, with many choosing to dress up, hoist flags and spend the holiday with their families. Sarwat Gilani posted a video of her husband and kids putting up flags and listening to Vital Signs’ ‘Dil Dil Pakistan’ — arguably the primary anthem for all Independence Day celebrations. Her message for the holiday hoped that the countless sacrifices people had given for the sake of the country would not go in vain and the people of Pakistan would honour them by building a country where “children feel safe”, “education is a right”, “women are respected” and where “honesty, kindness, tolerance and justice are stronger than hatred and fear”. Aiman Khan was also feeling the joy of freedom as she posted a video of herself singing along to ‘Dil Dil Pakistan’ on her Instagram account. Shehzad Roy upped the ante musically with a video of girls from a school run by his Zindagi Trust performing a heartwarming rendition of Mehdi Hassan’s classic ‘Yeh Watan Tumhara Hai’. Faran Tahir, celebrating Independence Day at home for the first time in 45 years, said he was doing so with “gratitude, pride and hope for all that Pakistan can become”. Nadia Jamil posted a clip of Independence Day fireworks and said the country was really its people. She hoped those people would work to make a “safe haven” where its children thrive and its people and animals feel safe. Adnan Siddiqui took a moment to remember the people taking part in Pakistan’s founding 79 years ago who had little apart from their “extraordinary conviction”. “They built something that could outlast them. It’s on us now to protect it, honour it and evolve it,” he wrote. Malala Yousafzai’s Independence Day wishes for Pakistan came with an appeal to invest in education. She said her recent interactions with the country’s youth made her excited and hopeful for the future. Ahsan Khan said Independence Day wasn’t just about raising flags and slogans, it was an opportunity for every Pakistani to look inwards and ask what they had done for their country. “The most beautiful expression of patriotism is that, wherever we may be, we increase Pakistan’s respect in the world with our successes and our actions,” he wrote. Celebrations were somewhat tempered this year after the country saw a number of horrific incidents of abuse against women and children in recent months, leading to many being mindful of that in their Independence Day messages. Merub Ali asked the all important question whether we truly were free when “women are scared to exist freely in their own country” and somehow everyone had accepted that reality as “normal”. “Don’t get me wrong. I love Pakistan. I love being Pakistani. This is my home… I owe so much of who I am today to this country and maybe that’s exactly why it hurts so much to watch what we’ve allowed it to become,” Ali said. “I’m incredibly proud to be Pakistani. I’m just heartbroken to be a Pakistani at a time where all of this has started feeling normal.” Zara Noor Abbas answered that question, saying we weren’t really free and today was actually about acknowledging the sacrifices of our forefathers and the hopes and dreams of the country’s children. Zhalay Sarhadi sang a soulful version of Nayyara Noor’s ‘Sohni Dharti’ with a note attached saying her “heart is heavy” this year. She prayed for justice, education, tolerance and the protection of the rights of women, children and animals in her country. Iqra Aziz’s Independence Day wish came with news of death and injuries in Karachi as a result of celebratory gunfire. Two people were killed in the metropolis and 94 were injured; the practice continues to be a regular occurrence despite a ban being in place. As the holiday continues, let us know how you’re celebrating and what you think Pakistanis should do for their country as we mark 79 years of independence. Happy Independence Day. Compunode.com Pvt. title: Bilal Lashari's The Legend of Maula Jatt bags two awards at Jackie Chan International Action Film Week - Culture - Images
description: The 2022 film won the Special Jury Award and Best Art Direction, after releasing in China this May.
content: The Legend of Maula Jatt, the blockbuster Pakistani film starring Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan and Hamza Ali Abbasi, has won two awards at the 7th Jackie Chan International Action Film Week. Director Bilal Lashari made the announcement on Instagram with a post celebrating the team and the continued success of the 2022 film. The Jackie Chan Action Film Week, now an award show and celebration of its own, was originally part of Shanghai International Film Festival, started by Chan in 2015. The fifth edition was held in 2019. In 2021, the sixth edition celebrated the top 10 classic Chinese action films. “Two awards, in the pouring rain, on a stage with Jackie Chan’s name on it. Still can’t quite believe this one,” he wrote. “ The Legend of Maula Jatt took home two honours at the closing ceremony of the 7th Jackie Chan International Action Film Week in Harbin, one of Asia’s biggest celebrations of action cinema. The Special Jury Award, and Best Art Direction,” he said, calling seeing his film alongside big names such as Mortal Kombat 2 and The Furious “wild”. “An open air stage in Harbin, thousands in the crowd, and rain coming down through all of it. It had been on and off all evening, then my turn to go up, and of course that’s just when the sky really opened up. Soaked by the time I reached the mic, a stranger holding an umbrella overhead, trophy dripping, the whole arena lit up behind the rain. As a director you dream of building moments like that on set. This one just happened,” Lashari wrote in his caption. He said the Art Direction award was special to him because it wasn’t his — it belonged instead to Namsa Abbasi and Hamza Bajwa. “What these two built wasn’t just sets and design, it was an entire world, and every scene of the film breathes because of them. Accepting it on their behalf, in the rain, on that stage… I wish they’d been there. This is yours. Fully deserved.” He also gave a shoutout to producer Ammara Hikmat, who wasn’t in Harbin to receive the award either. “We felt your absence up there.” The Jackie Chan International Action Film Week is named after the Chinese action star who inspired millions of starry-eyed children to get into action. One of those children was Lashari, who said he grew up on Chan’s films. “So to be on a stage with his name on it, representing Pakistan, and then to shake his hand and have him congratulate us in person, I never pictured any of this when we started,” he said. “There’s really nothing that pulls people from every corner of the world together like a good action film. No subtitles needed, you just feel it. Thank you to Mr Jackie Chan, the organisers, and the jury for putting action, and the people who make it, on a stage as magnificent as this.” He also thanked producer Nadeem Mandviwalla and his wife, calling them his “partners in crime through all these China adventures”. “To our entire team, thank you. Every bit of this is yours. And to Pakistan, this one’s for you.” While the celebration of Maula Jatt in China may seem rather delayed, the film only released in the country this past May. Lashari penned a note on Instagram after the Beijing premiere of the film, lauding the warmth they received from the press, the industry and the people in the room, something he “genuinely wasn’t prepared for”. The love for the film in Pakistan is overwhelming, he mused, but different. “It’s wrapped up in everything else. The stars, the story, the years of waiting. Sometimes, as the director, you almost disappear inside all of that. Which is beautiful. But it’s a different feeling.” In Beijing, none of that context existed, Lashari said. “They didn’t know our actors. They didn’t know our industry. They came in with nothing. And what came back was something pure. Just two of us who travelled a long way to share it, a director and a distributor, received like we’d brought something that mattered.” That love and warmth reminded him of something he’d started to take for granted. “No platform, no algorithm, no TikTok can do what a cinema does. A darkened room, strangers sitting together, a story unfolding. Last night reminded me why cinema is cinema.” The film stars Fawad and Mahira, Humaima Malick, Hamza Ali Abbasi, Gohar Rasheed, Faris Shafi and Ali Azmat, and is a reboot of the 1979 cult classic Maula Jatt , reimagining Punjab’s own superhero for a world audience. The movie made Rs1 billion at the domestic box office and $10 million at the worldwide box office, as of January 2023, making it one of, if not the highest performing Pakistani films ever. title: Sania Saeed, Maria Wasti, Mehmood Aslam among artists receiving civil awards on March 23 - Celebrity - Images
description: tA number of writers, poets and athletes will also be conferred awards.
content: As part of the country’s Independence Day celebrations, the Government of Pakistan announced the annual list of civil honours. The awardees, who are being recognised for their services to Pakistan in a range of fields, will receive their awards on March 23 (Pakistan Day) next year. Of a total of 372 awards, 54 will be presented for contributions to the arts, 29 for literature and nine for sports. Notable awardees from the list include actors Sania Saeed, Maria Wasti and Mahmood Aslam; musicians Shiraz Uppal and Zulfiqar Jabbar Khan (Xulfi) and TV host Shafat Ali. title: 4 artists examine hidden lives embedded within objects, images and memories at Canvas Gallery - Culture - Images
description: Minaa Haroon, Muhammad Muzammil Khan, Rafay Talpur and Raheela Abro displayed their work in Time and Traces.
content: Artists Minaa Haroon, Muhammad Muzammil Khan, Rafay Talpur and Raheela Abro each translate the ideas of inherited objects, artistic legacies, memories of confinement and the precariousness of nourishment through a distinctive visual language in their exhibition ‘Time and Traces’ at Canvas Gallery. Although the concerns of these four artists could hardly be more different at first glance, yet they overlap in their preoccupation with what time leaves behind. The jewellery forms of Haroon are unmistakable, almost floating within dense, radiating patterns. Beginning with pieces inherited from her mother, she casts, carves and gilds their forms, embedding them in handmade paper and intricate geometric patterns. The colour of the ground intensifies the gold and dark blue motifs, while the rough edges of the handmade paper deliberately contrast with the precision of the miniature-like ornamentation. The result is apparent in works where necklaces and pendants appear almost suspended within radiating fields of turquoise, orange, blue and gold. Minaa’s miniature training is apparent in her precision, but the layered paper, gold leaf and material experimentation take the work beyond conventional miniature painting. The jewellery remains recognisable as an object, while simultaneously becoming part of an abstract visual field. The heirloom is neither preserved intact nor simply depicted — it is transformed into something closer to a map of memory. To my mind, it is this transformation of adornment into something approaching an abstract topography that is one of the more distinctive aspects of the exhibition. Four artists examined the hidden lives embedded within objects, images and memories at a recent show in Karachi Muzammil also engages with inheritance, though his is an explicitly artistic legacy. His father, Muhammad Rustam Khan, is a remarkably talented self-taught artist. The influence of his hyperrealistic portraits and the use of vibrant colours is evident in his son’s work. Muzammil responds by pushing against the restrained conventions of miniature painting and manipulating layers of wasli to create relief and depth. His ode to his father through these portraits is technically impressive, but it is the contrast between faces of different ages that gives the series greater resonance. In one, a young woman, wrapped in a warm, ochre burqa looks away with an almost cinematic intensity. In another, an elderly man in a blue kurta and patterned turban confronts the viewer with a deeply furrowed face and meticulously rendered hands. Smoothness and weathering, youth and age become, quite literally, studies in the passage of time. The most austere works in the exhibition are by Rafay. His compositions in stark black-and-white palette in drypoint (a printmaking technique using a sharp pointed tool to essentially ‘gouge’ a line into the metal), which initially appear to be simple studies of shadows, acquire a psychological dimension when one delves deeper into his intensely personal and disturbing emotional past. His childhood experiences of punishment, confinement and darkness at a madrassa [seminary] inform this body of monochromatic works, in which black fields are interrupted by narrow passages of white. The white comes from the emotional release associated with light. In one striking composition, vertical white strips penetrate rounded black forms, evoking bars, apertures or shafts of light. The imagery is deliberately sparse and this restraint is its strength. Rather than illustrating confinement, Rafay creates a psychological sensation of it, making the viewer conscious of how little light is available and how significant its presence becomes. Raheela turns to something far more familiar: the apple and orange. In The Weight of the Rind, fruit becomes a vehicle for considering food security, inequality, sustainability and survival. She places the fruit almost ceremonially within an ornate frame, and her small, box-like presentations of an orange and an apple are particularly intriguing. Their almost shrine-like or specimen-case presentation makes ordinary fruit appear precious, vulnerable and strangely isolated, resembling specimens being preserved or objects whose availability can no longer be taken for granted. The enclosing frames reinforce the ideas of preservation and scarcity, and the works are most persuasive when their symbolism is understated. An apple, isolated within an ornate frame against a green ground, acquires an almost precious status. The tension between abundance and fragility gives these modest subjects a wider significance. Despite their disparate approaches, the four artists make ‘Time and Traces’ a coherent exhibition. Jewellery, faces, shadows and fruit become repositories of experience. The ‘traces’ are sometimes intimate and personal, sometimes inherited and sometimes connected to larger anxieties about survival. What lingers most is the idea that nothing remains untouched by time: objects are transformed, faces weather, memories persist, light penetrates darkness and even something as ordinary as fruit can come to signify an uncertain future. ‘Time and Traces’ was on display at Canvas Gallery in Karachi from July 28-August 6, 2026 Originally published in Dawn, EOS, August 9th, 2026 Compunode.com Pvt. title: LHC upholds divorced woman’s right to house as dower - Pakistan - DAWN.COM
description: Dismisses husband’s appeal against lower courts’ decisions.
content: Get the latest news and updates from Dawn • Dismisses husband’s appeal against lower courts’ decisions • Rules technical objections over ordinary stamp paper cannot defeat proven matrimonial rights LAHORE: The Lahore High Court has upheld concurrent judgements of two lower courts granting a divorced woman possession of a house as dower (haq mehr), ruling that a separately executed dower agreement was valid and enforceable even though the property was not mentioned in the nikahnama (marriage certificate). Justice Sajid Mehmood Sethi of the LHC dismissed a petition filed by Muhammad Khan, who had challenged decisions of a family court and an appellate court in Chiniot in favour of his former wife, Anwar Bibi. The woman claimed that on the day of their marriage in 2017, the petitioner executed an agreement promising her a constructed five-marla house in Canada Colony, Chiniot, as dower and also undertook to pay Rs300,000 in the event of divorce. After the marriage ended in 2021, she sought recovery of the house, its market value, maintenance for the iddat period and the contractual amount. However, the husband denied executing the agreement, alleging that it was fabricated and asserting that the property belonged to his first wife. He argued that the agreement was written on ordinary stamp paper instead of an e-stamp paper and that the nikahnama mentioned dower of only Rs5,000. Rejecting these arguments, Justice Sethi held that family courts have exclusive jurisdiction over dower disputes and observed that the agreement clearly fixed the house as haq mehr. The judge noted that both attesting witnesses to the agreement testified in support of its execution and remained unshaken during cross-examination. He further observed that the petitioner opposed forensic examination of his signatures and thumb impression on the document, a conduct that justified drawing an adverse inference against him. “The refusal of the petitioner to permit forensic examination substantially erodes the credibility of his plea of fabrication and lends support to the concurrent findings recorded by the courts below,” Justice Sethi held. The judge ruled that under settled principles of Muslim law, dower may be fixed before, at the time of, or even after marriage, and may also be enhanced through a separate agreement. He said the nikahnama was not the exclusive record of dower arrangements and that a separate written instrument could validly coexist with it. The judge also rejected the husband’s contention that the agreement was invalid because it had been executed on ordinary stamp paper, holding that technical objections regarding the form of documentation could not defeat substantive matrimonial rights once the transaction had been independently proved. Justice Sethi observed that the argument that the woman did not assert her claim during the subsistence of marriage was legally untenable. “In the social realities of our society, many women refrain from demanding dower during continuance of marriage for emotional, domestic and societal reasons. Such restraint cannot legally be construed against them,” the judge maintained, adding that the right to recover dower survives dissolution of marriage and remains enforceable in accordance with law. Finding no illegality, misreading of evidence or jurisdictional defect in the concurrent findings of the lower courts, the LHC judge dismissed the petition and maintained the decree awarding the house to the former wife as dower. Published in Dawn, May 31th, 2026 Wajih Ahmad Sheikh is a Lahore-based correspondent for Dawn with over two decades of experience covering legal affairs and judicial developments. title: Zahabia Khozema's exhibition at Vasl Gallery explores the power of memory - Culture - Images
description: By preserving the emotional geography of a place, the artist suggests that remembering itself can become a way of resisting disappearance.
content: There is something unsettling about places that continue to exist only in memory. They linger somewhere between reality and imagination, carrying fragments of lives that can no longer be revisited. Zahabia Khozema’s ‘A Memory Catcher Visited My Town’ is built around this fragile space between remembering and forgetting. Inspired by the recollections of a boy who grew up in an industrial town in central Punjab, this exhibition at Vasl Gallery becomes less a record of a disappearing place and more a meditation on belonging, loss and the landscapes we carry within us. The artist’s statement introduces a stone-crusher, a goat-grazer and a coal-miner awaiting the arrival of a “memory catcher.” It unfolds almost like folklore, yet beneath its poetic language lies a sobering reality. The town gradually disappears under the pressures of capitalist expansion, economic violence and climate change. Rather than documenting this transformation literally, Khozema explores what remains when homes, communities and identities begin to dissolve. This sense of abandonment is particularly evident in How Many Times Did You Pass by This House?, where an empty dwelling stands as more than an architectural form. Stripped of human presence, it suggests that buildings, much like people, retain the memories of those who once inhabited them. Through luminous colours and dreamlike settings, Zahabia Khozema explores how memory preserves places long after they have disappeared from the physical world Similarly, Let Us Meet Here Again, with its solitary chair placed within an expansive landscape, transforms an ordinary object into a poignant symbol of absence. The chair inspires conversations that never took place, people who never returned and places that continue to wait long after they have been forgotten. The paintings rarely feel tied to a specific geography. Rivers, abandoned houses, flowering trees and open landscapes drift between dream and recollection, occupying a liminal territory where certainty gives way to sensation. Rather than reconstructing a town with documentary precision, Khozema paints the emotional architecture of remembrance. The viewer is left navigating spaces that feel familiar without ever being fully identifiable, as though assembled from scattered fragments of childhood. Perhaps the exhibition’s most compelling quality is its use of colour. A body of work addressing displacement, environmental decline and erasure might be expected to rely on subdued tones, yet Khozema embraces intensely saturated blues, luminous pinks, violets and fiery oranges. In When the Mountains Called for Us, broad, expressive passages of warm colour, interrupted by seemingly unfinished forms and abrupt gestures, lend the work an almost dreamlike quality. The looseness of the composition depicts the fragmented way memory often survives. Likewise, What Was Behind This is dominated by glowing reds and magentas, interrupted only by delicate passages of cool blue, suggesting that warmth and melancholy can exist within the same remembered moment. Materiality further strengthens this atmosphere. Working with oil pastel and oil sticks, Khozema builds dense, tactile surfaces that reward prolonged looking. Thick deposits of pigment, energetic scribbles and layered marks prevent the paintings from becoming overly polished. While deeply personal, the exhibition also gestures towards wider political realities. The vanished town is not presented as the inevitable consequence of time but as the result of systems that value extraction over communities and development over continuity. Climate change further deepens this vulnerability, reminding us that landscapes and livelihoods often disappear together. Although the exhibition draws upon themes of capitalist erasure, economic violence and environmental decline, these ideas remain understated within the paintings themselves. Rather than confronting the viewer directly, Khozema allows them to emerge gradually through atmosphere and memory, inviting viewers to feel their emotional weight before recognising their broader social implications. ‘A Memory Catcher Visited My Town’ ultimately becomes an act of resistance. By preserving the emotional geography of a place, Khozema suggests that remembering itself can become a way of resisting disappearance. The exhibition stays long after one leaves the gallery, not simply because it reminds of what has been lost, but because it asks what remains when an entire town survives only in the memories of those who once called it home. ‘A Memory Catcher Visited My Town’ was on display at Vasl Gallery in Karachi from July 28-August 7, 2026 Originally published in Dawn, EOS, August 9th, 2026 Compunode.com Pvt. title: Filmmaker Shahood Alvi says people should be ashamed of twisting his words on social media - Celebrity - Images
description: Viral clips of the filmmaker's comments about men not wanting to talk to their wives have caused an uproar.
content: Actor and filmmaker Shahood Alvi says people on the internet are taking his words out of context and misrepresenting his views on women after clips surfaced of his appearance on Monday’s episode of Good Morning Pakistan . In his post on Tuesday, Alvi claimed his words had been twisted and that what people on social media chose to focus on were not his views, but those of “the majority of men in our society”. “This has nothing to do with my views on women,” he explained. The filmmaker said he believed in empowering and supporting strong and confident women, which reflected in how he treated his wife and daughter. He said he provided his wife “with all the household help she needs” and respected everything she had done for him. Alvi came under fire for his statements made during a programme themed around marital disputes. A caller to the show complained that her husband used his phone excessively after work and failed to pay attention to her at home. In response, host Nida Yasir quipped that when her husband is too engrossed in his phone, she just goes into another room and sends him a voice message with whatever it was she needed to tell him. Alvi — after jokingly suggesting that her husband might be cheating on her — told the woman she should do something to make her husband pay attention to her, like making him a good meal. Actor Leyla Zuberi, who was sitting next to him, suggested she should dress up and do make-up before her husband comes home, as that’s what her mother used to do. Actor Fahima Awan, who was also on the show, said she would “side with the men here” and suggested that the woman’s husband may be in no mood to chat after a long day at work. She said maybe reading more and knowing more about the world would help the caller engage her spouse in a more intellectually stimulating conversation. Later, as the host and the other guests were discussing the significance of physical and intellectual grooming, Alvi chimed in saying a husband may not be thrilled to talk to his wife if “he comes home and she’s smelling of ginger and garlic”. He said this was in contrast to the women he interacts with in the workplace who “are wearing perfume as they work alongside him”. Responding to the backlash over the above statement, Alvi on Tuesday said: “Shame on people who try to tarnish one’s reputation just for views.” Compunode.com Pvt. Ltd. title: Are Patangeer's Amtul Baweja and Fahad Tariq hosting the first Pakistan Influencer Awards? - Local - Images
description: The awards are an industry-led initiative to recognise Pakistani content creators.
content: Amtul Baweja and Fahad Tariq — the content creator duo behind the vlog Patangeer — are set to host the inaugural edition of the Pakistan Influencer Awards. In a reel shared on their Instagram page, Baweja said the couple had spent eight years in content creation, becoming part of “an incredible community” of digital creators and influencers. She said they didn’t know then that “one day, we’d be standing on stage, representing this very community and hosting the first Pakistan Influencer Awards.” The content creator said the initiative was driven by the industry and that it is “a great way to acknowledge Pakistani content creators and the work we’ve done in the past years.” The Pakistan Influencer Awards are scheduled to be held on November 7. At an event on July 27, the initiative’s chief curator, Talha Aslam, said they wanted to set some “guardrails” and build a “culture” for content creation to thrive in Pakistan. Over 30 different awards will be given out, including Creator of the Year and Emerging Creator awards for Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. Separate category awards will be given to creators for their work in areas like lifestyle, beauty, fashion, travel, fitness, entertainment, gaming, parenting, music and many more. The awards will be given based on the results of an extensive process. The top 20 creators qualifying for each award will be filtered through an algorithm — with a market survey conducted to validate the results — after which a jury of established content creators will choose the top 10. A second jury of marketing and advertising professionals will then select the top five, after which the names will be put to a public vote, expected to be held online in October. Compunode.com Pvt. title: Bilal Maqsood's children's show Pakkay Dost will return for its fourth season on Aug 22 - Culture - Images
description: The upcoming season will teach kids about exercise and being kind to animals.
content: Bilal Maqsood is set to release the fourth season of his popular puppet show Pakkay Dost on August 22, the musician announced on Wednesday. In a reel shared to his own Instagram account as well as the show’s, Maqsood reiterated his earlier point about how his goal for the programme was to make the kind of “healthy, wholesome” content in Urdu that would make the language “cool and relevant” for kids. Actor Syra Yousuf, who stars in the show as Mimi, also appears in the reel. The singer said there were some very interesting songs in this season, about things like exercise and vegetables to promote a healthier lifestyle. He also said there was a song about what different bones are called in Urdu. Kindness and compassion towards animals are also themes discussed on the show. Maqsood asked parents to watch the show with their kids, since he designed it with both groups in mind. “When I write, compose the songs, [I feel like] there’s no point if I am not having fun,” he said. The singer said anyone who hadn’t seen the show yet should start from the first season. “There are around 50+ songs that will have you learning things and your kids will be learning to love Urdu.” Pakkay Dost has been trying to make children appreciate Pakistan’s culture and languages throughout its three-season run, with past collaborations with ConnectHear and the Government of Sindh making the show available in Sindhi and sign language . The show is available to watch for free on YouTube. Compunode.com Pvt. Ltd. ( www.compunode.com ).Designed for Dawn .

title: Disney reveals X-Men cast, slate of sequels at D23 fan event - Culture - Images
description: Footage from Avengers: Doomsday was also previewed at the event.
content: Adam Driver, Inde Navarrette and Sadie Sink will be among those joining the cast of Marvel’s next X-Men movie, Disney announced at its biennial D23 fan gathering in California on Friday. Marvel Studios chief Kevin Feige took to the stage at Honda Centre on the first night of the three-day convention to give more than 10,000 fans a sneak peek of the so-far untitled film, which is slated for a May 2028 release. Sink will reprise her role in Spider-Man: Brand New Day as Jean Grey, while Navarrette will play Rogue. The cast also includes Kit Connor (Cyclops), Samara Weaving (Emma Frost), Christopher Abbott (Professor Xavier) and Maya Boyd (Storm). Driver, who joined the event via video, will play the villain Nathaniel Milbury. “Kevin and I have been talking for years about maybe joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe. And I think we finally found the perfect film at the perfect time,” Driver said. Feige also showed footage from Avengers: Doomsday , set to be released in December, which will bring together the Avengers, the Fantastic Four, X-Men and Wakandan warriors in an epic clash against the evil Doctor Doom, played by Robert Downey Jr. Another highlight was the first look at Ryan Gosling in Lucasfilm’s Star Wars: Starfighter , which will hit the big screen in 2027 to coincide with the 50th anniversary of Star Wars . Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro, who took over in March, kickstarted this year’s D23 event, which has become a platform for studios to showcase their latest projects alongside stars, creatives and directors. Pixar offered previews of its Italian fable Gatto and supernatural tale Ghost Market , as well as The Incredibles 3 and Coco 2 . Other sequels unveiled include Lilo & Stitch 2 , Ice Age: Boiling Point and Frozen 3 , promoted by stars Kristen Bell, Idina Menzel and Josh Gad. “Everything’s a sequel here,” said attendee Gary Aurin, who came to D23 with his son. “That’s Disney, so you just gotta get used to it.” Director Jon Favreau took to the stage to introduce Oswald the Lucky Rabbit , a mini-series to debut next year on the Disney+ platform. The cartoon rabbit Oswald preceded Mickey Mouse and was created by Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks in 1927 for Universal Pictures. Disney acquired the rights to the character in 2006. D23 will wrap up on Sunday. Compunode.com Pvt. Ltd. ( www.compunode.com ).Designed for Dawn .

title: Pro-Palestine campaigners urge boycott of Spider-Man: Brand New Day over producer's ties to Israel - Culture - Images
description: Producer Avi Arad, an Israeli citizen and former IDF member, has rejected criticism of the war on Gaza.
content: Pro-Palestinian campaigners in Lebanon, Jordan and elsewhere in the Arab world have called for a boycott of Spider-Man: Brand New Day over producer Avi Arad’s support for Israel and his rejection of criticism directed at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during the war on Gaza . The Campaign to Boycott Supporters of Israel in Lebanon urged audiences not to purchase tickets for the film, arguing that financially supporting a production involving figures who have publicly backed Israel amounts to “cultural normalisation”. “Do we want to support a production involving individuals who have publicly expressed political support for Israel?” the group said in a social media statement ahead of the film’s release. The campaign called on the public to avoid paid screenings and said its position reflected its opposition to normalising Israel or its policies. In Jordan, the Taharrak anti-normalisation group issued a separate statement calling for the film to be boycotted and excluded from the schedules of Jordanian cinemas. The group also urged the Jordanian Artists Syndicate, cinema operators and other relevant bodies to take a position against its screening. The calls have since been amplified by activists and content creators in other Arab countries. Spider-Man: Brand New Day , released internationally on July 31, stars Tom Holland as Peter Parker and is directed by Destin Daniel Cretton. Marvel lists Arad as one of its four producers alongside Kevin Feige, Amy Pascal and Rachel O’Connor. The campaign focuses on Arad’s political record rather than the film’s plot or its other cast and crew members. Arad, a former Marvel Studios chief who holds Israeli and US citizenship, served in the Israeli military between 1965 and 1968 and was involved in the 1967 Six-Day War. In a 2024 letter published by entertainment news outlet TheWrap , Arad rebuked then-US Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer after the senator described Netanyahu as an obstacle to peace and called for Israel to hold new elections. “It’s not your war. It is not your country. And it is not you who is at risk,” Arad wrote, arguing that Schumer had no right to influence Israel’s electoral process. He also described himself as a proud former member of the Israeli military and rejected Schumer’s position on a ceasefire. Campaigners say those statements demonstrate Arad’s support for Israel’s conduct during the Gaza war and argue that ticket purchases contribute financially to a production associated with him. The effect of the campaign on attendance remains unclear. The film continued to screen in Lebanon despite the boycott call, with a representative of the Grand Cinemas chain telling Lebanese publication L’Orient Today shortly after its release that demand remained high. title: Pop star Selena Gomez, mother, former business partner sued for investment-related fraud - Culture - Images
description: Investors in the singer's mental health startup allege they were deceived about the company's standing and her role in it.
content: A number of investors in Wondermind — a mental health startup started by American pop star Selena Gomez — have sued the star, her mother Mandy Teefey and business partner Daniella Pierson, claiming they were misled about company’s business and Gomez’s involvement. According to a complaint filed in a court in Delaware on Thursday, the trio “falsely represented” the company to two groups of investors who claim they put almost $1.2 million into the company, TMZ reported. Founded in 2021, Wondermind’s website says it gives its audience “easy, doable ways to put your mental fitness first every day”. Gomez is listed as a co-founder while Teefey is listed as CEO; Pierson left the company in 2023 after reported disagreements with Teefey. The three are being sued for securities fraud, common law fraud, breach of contract and other claims, with plaintiffs alleging that “for three years, while the company quietly collapsed around them, not one of its founders, officers, or directors said a word to the investors whose money was funding the collapse”. Their lawsuit says the complainants were led to believe Wondermind had partnerships with companies such as JP Morgan along with “advertising deals, celebrity cover stories, and a groundbreaking app”. “The partnerships did not exist. The initiatives never materialised. The app was never built,” the investors alleged. The investors were alerted of the company’s troubles by a report published in September by The Cut , which detailed internal power struggles, Teefey’s “gross mismanagement” of the company and Gomez’s “abject dereliction of her duties” and “her active efforts to distance herself from it”, the complaint said. Investors say they sent an email to Teefey in November asking for their investment to be returned. Teefey sent an email saying she would respond in 10 days’ time, but “never substantively responded to the notice”. In April, she responded to another notice saying she “thought we returned your investment” and said this was a matter for “Selena’s legal team” when pushed further on the matter. Eventually, Teefey said Wondermind had created an escrow account to assist in returning the investment. However, according to the complaint, “when the plaintiffs repeatedly followed up with Teefey to obtain details about that purported escrow account, Teefey disappeared”. According to the investors, there was no escrow account and this was a continuation of “years-long scheme of deceit” carried out by Gomez, Teefey and Pierson. The plaintiffs are seeking the return of their initial investment, as well as damages and legal fees. Compunode.com Pvt. Ltd. ( www.compunode.com ).Designed for Dawn .

title: Review: Nadia Hashmi's City of Widows gives you a glimpse into the fall of Kabul through a woman's eyes - Culture - Images
description: The novel traces what it meant to be an Afghan woman when the world decided the war was over.
content: In August 2021, the world watched Kabul fall. As Taliban fighters streamed into the presidential palace and desperate crowds swarmed the airport, the images broadcast across the globe captured chaos, but not its texture — the specific, private terror of women who had spent two decades building careers, raising daughters, and imagining futures that could be erased in an afternoon. Nadia Hashimi’s City of Widows steps into that silence. It’s a novel that refuses the long shot of history in favour of the close-up, tracing what it meant to be an Afghan woman when the world decided the war was over. The prologue opens like a thriller. A dozen women are crammed into a stifling room on a hilltop outside Kabul, the settlement known as Zanabad, the City of Widows. Their leader, Kobra, fixes her gaze on Marjan, a newcomer with a soldier’s bearing and a daughter to protect. “Marjan,” she says, “You have not been honest with me.” The sentence hangs. An infant swallows a cry. Bodies press against clay walls. Then Marjan’s teenage daughter, Hawa, steps forward and speaks: “My mother has made a lot of enemies in her life. … But I’m the reason we are in danger.” In a few compressed pages, Hashimi establishes the novel’s central truth — that survival depends on the stories women tell, and on whether those stories can hold up under pressure. The narrative moves between two timelines. In the present, August 2021, Marjan is a former operative of the Female Tactical Platoon, an elite unit trained by American Special Forces to conduct night raids. She knows that the Taliban will hunt down soldiers like her. She needs visas, safe passage and a way out for Hawa. Interwoven with this race against time is the story of her past: a girl named Rahima, who was married at 13 to a warlord and escaped his compound while pregnant and rebuilt herself as Marjan, borrowing the name from a wounded lion at the Kabul Zoo. The dual structure asks a hard question: what safety is possible when the institutions meant to protect women — the shelter, the military, the foreign forces — dissolve overnight? Hashimi’s prose is at its most devastating when it fixes on the body in pain. Early in the novel, teenage Rahima is examined by a doctor who confirms the pregnancy forced upon her. “Rahima let out a howl that slipped under the closed door, out of the clinic, and into the street, where it caused two women to pause their steps, but only briefly. As if they had heard a car honk or a door slam. The cry of a girl wronged by the universe was hardly remarkable.” The passage is remarkable precisely because it refuses to amplify the scream. It notes how quickly the world absorbs a girl’s grief and moves on. This documentary restraint is sustained through the novel’s most harrowing set piece, the Abbey Gate bombing. Hashimi describes a dead child with clinical precision: “Brown curls cling to her forehead. Her hair is spread on the earth.” She does not tell the reader what to feel. The flatness becomes its own accusation. In contrast, the 2021 sections sometimes labour under the weight of explanation. When characters debate visa categories or dissect the mechanics of the American withdrawal agreement, the dialogue flattens into information. I found the novel most persuasive when it trusted objects and gestures — a half-dozen bangles, a plastic water bottle twisted in nervous hands, a notebook with a ledger for a rubab — to carry the political argument. These small things speak louder than the speeches. Music is the novel’s most carefully sustained motif. Hawa studies the rubab at a Kabul institute, and her lessons with Ustad Rafiqi are among the book’s finest scenes. When Hawa stumbles over a passage, her teacher stops her: “The only thing worse than a shoddy note is no note at all. … Do not sacrifice an entire song for one wayward note. The music you are playing is older than our years combined. It has survived wars and drought and fickle hearts. It will survive your choppy renditions as well.” The lines double as an artistic credo for the novel itself, which insists that flawed, persistent creation matters more than the silence the Taliban would impose. When Hawa later plays her flute to catch a marine’s attention at the airport, music becomes survival in a literal key. The mother-daughter relationship is the novel’s emotional core. Marjan’s love is rendered as a ferocious inventory: new sneakers, a winter coat, a bar of lavender soap left behind. Yet the intimacy sometimes stays at arm’s length; we see Marjan’s devotion more through her budgeting and her vigilance than through sustained, unguarded exchanges with her daughter. The exception is the prologue, where Hawa’s declaration earns its force through everything the novel has withheld. What Hashimi understands with terrifying clarity is that the end of a war is not the end of danger for women; it is simply its reconfiguration. This insight pulses beneath every scene. When the Americans withdraw, the threat Marjan faces is not new. It is the same patriarchal violence she fled a decade earlier, now wearing the legitimacy of state power. The Female Tactical Platoon, which offered the brief illusion of institutional protection, evaporates. The shelter that once saved her can no longer guarantee anything. Hashimi refuses the consolations of rescue. The airport sequences are suffused not with the romance of escape but with the grinding logistics of survival, the slow accumulation of small betrayals and sudden losses that define humanitarian catastrophe. In the context of Hashimi’s career, City of Widows marks a maturation. Her earlier novel, The Pearl That Broke Its Shell, explored the tradition of bacha posh with evident research that sometimes sat uneasily on the surface. Here, history is absorbed into character and scene. The closer, more fragmented third-person perspective mirrors the characters’ precarious hold on safety and identity. The reader is never entirely comfortable, and that discomfort is the point. If the novel has a weakness, it is a tendency to name its own themes. Words like resilience and resistance appear with a frequency that risks dulling their edge. Hashimi does not need them. When Soraya, Marjan’s fellow soldier, defends her right to wear lipstick on a night mission — “if I die, I die pretty” — the politics are unmistakable without commentary. I wished the novel had allowed more such moments to speak for themselves, trusting the reader to recognise rebellion in a tube of lipstick, defiance in a rubab string. The epigraph is drawn from Rumi: “Ever since I was cut from my bed of reeds / My song can elicit human tears.” Hashimi treats separation as a formal problem. Her characters are severed from names, homes, families, countries, and the novel’s fractured timeline enacts that severance at the level of structure. It is an elegant solution, though it occasionally slows the narrative. City of Widows is a novel for readers who believe fiction can engage with contemporary crisis without abandoning its obligations to art. It will resonate with those who admired the moral sweep of Khaled Hosseini’s work but longed for a more granular immersion in female interiority. Hashimi offers no easy redemption. She turns her characters into allegories of nothing. I closed the book not with a tidy political thesis but with a sensory residue: the grain of a rubab’s note, the scent of lavender soap, the weight of a water bottle twisted in a soldier’s tired hands. These are small things, but in Hashimi’s hands, they are enough. Compunode.com Pvt. Ltd. ( www.compunode.com ).Designed for Dawn .

title: Bangladesh beat Pakistan by 78 runs to clinch Test series 2-0 - Sport - DAWN.COM
description: The victory is Bangladesh’s first Test series win at home against Pakistan and a second successive sweep after their 2-0 triumph on Pakistani soil in 2024.
content: Get the latest news and updates from Dawn Spinner Taijul Islam took six wickets to lead Bangladesh to a 78-run win over Pakistan in the second Test and clinch a famous 2-0 series win on Wednesday. Pakistan, who started the fifth day on 316-7 while chasing a record 437, were bowled out for 328 in the first session in Sylhet after Mohammad Rizwan hit a valiant 94. It was Bangladesh’s first Test series win at home against Pakistan and a second successive sweep after their 2-0 triumph on Pakistani soil in 2024. Wicketkeeper Rizwan kept Pakistan in the hunt for an unlikely win with a 166-ball stay after the visitors had slumped to 162-5 on day four. Rizwan put on an eighth-wicket partnership of 54 with overnight partner Sajid Khan, who made 28. Taijul broke through to dismiss Sajid for his 18th Test five-wicket haul and Shoriful Islam had Rizwan caught in the next over to end Pakistan’s resistance. Taijul took the final wicket of Khurram Shahzad to return figures of 6-120 and trigger Bangladesh celebrations. The left-arm spinner also took 3-67 during Pakistan’s first innings 232. Bangladesh wicketkeeper Litton Das scored 126 in their first-innings 278. Veteran batsman Mushfiqur Rahim scored 137 in the second to guide Bangladesh to 390, with contributions from Mahmudul Hasan Joy (52) and Litton (69). Bangladesh, led by Najmul Hossain Shanto, won the opening Test by 104 runs. Speaking after the match, captain Shaan Masood conceded that there were “a lot of mistakes”. “There were things we didn’t do well enough in the first three innings and that’s why the effort on the fourth and fifth day didn’t really materialise into a win,” he said, according to ESPNcricinfo . He added that Test cricket was “unforgiving” and played by the “best of the best”. “You’re not going to get any easy games, you have to grind results out, and that’s what you have to do as a side,” he said.
